title: What Entrepreneurship Is
in30Seconds: Entrepreneurship is action aimed at creating value by creating or expanding economic activity, often through a new product, process, market, or way of organizing work. It is not a job title, a company size, or a promise of profit. An entrepreneur acts while important outcomes are still uncertain, makes choices with limited information, and is accountable for learning from the results.
whyItMatters: A precise definition keeps later entrepreneurship topics from turning into slogans. It helps you distinguish an idea from the work of pursuing it, innovation from mere novelty, and ownership from entrepreneurial action. That distinction matters in college cases, workplaces, nonprofits, and businesses: a founder, an employee, or a team can act entrepreneurially, while a new or small firm may simply operate an established model. It also makes risk talk more honest. Entrepreneurship involves uncertainty and trade-offs; it does not guarantee growth, investment, or personal wealth.
learningObjectives: Define entrepreneurship as value-creating action rather than a personality type or business size.
Distinguish entrepreneur, entrepreneurial activity, and entrepreneurship.
Explain why entrepreneurial action occurs under uncertainty and does not guarantee success.
Compare entrepreneurship with small-business ownership using a qualified, non-binary distinction.
Apply the definition to identify entrepreneurial action inside or outside a newly founded firm.

collegeVersion.heading: A definition centered on action and value
collegeVersion.body:
Entrepreneurship is best treated as a phenomenon of action, not as a badge someone earns by calling themself a founder. The OECD–Eurostat Entrepreneurship Indicators Programme defines entrepreneurial activity as human action in pursuit of value through the creation or expansion of economic activity, including through identifying and exploiting new products, processes, or markets. That framing gives us three useful pieces. First, there is action: noticing a possibility is not yet entrepreneurship unless someone commits effort and resources to pursue it. Second, the aim is value. Value can include revenue, but the OECD notes that entrepreneurial outcomes need not be financial wealth alone; employment, social outcomes, or environmental outcomes may matter too. Third, the activity changes or extends economic activity. A venture might introduce an offering, redesign a process, open a new market, or grow an existing operation in a new direction.

The related words should not be collapsed. An entrepreneur is a person pursuing value-creating activity. Entrepreneurial activity is what people do in that pursuit. Entrepreneurship is the broader phenomenon associated with that activity. This distinction is useful because it separates a person from an act and an act from a social or economic pattern. It also prevents a common error: treating a business registration, a pitch deck, or a clever idea as sufficient evidence of entrepreneurship. Those may be inputs or artifacts. The defining feature is purposeful action that seeks to create value in a setting where the outcome is not already settled.

collegeVersion.heading: Uncertainty, risk, and responsible judgment
collegeVersion.body:
Entrepreneurial action takes place before the actor knows how customers, costs, competitors, regulations, collaborators, or technology will develop. That is uncertainty: relevant outcomes and their likelihoods are not fully known. Risk is related but not identical. A risk may be a downside exposure that can be estimated or partly controlled; uncertainty also includes surprises that resist reliable prediction. In practice, the two often appear together. A team can budget for an equipment purchase, for example, but it cannot know in advance exactly how a changed process will perform or how others will respond to it.

This does not make entrepreneurship reckless. OpenStax describes calculated risk as a willingness to act after due diligence—research and investigation intended to inform decisions and reduce avoidable exposure. The important word is reduce, not remove. Careful analysis, contracts, testing, insurance, savings, and staged commitments can change an exposure, but none turns an uncertain outcome into a guarantee. A good entrepreneurship analysis therefore asks what decision is being made, what value is sought, what is known, what remains uncertain, whose resources are at stake, and what evidence would change the next decision. It does not mistake confidence for evidence or a favorable result for proof that the original choice was safe.

Failure and entrepreneurship are also separate questions. In the OECD framework, people whose ventures fail can still have engaged in entrepreneurial activity; success is not built into the definition. This is not an excuse to ignore consequences. It is a reminder to evaluate both the quality of a decision at the time it was made and the result that followed. The later lessons on finding business ideas and problem identification take up how possibilities and needs may be explored. This lesson establishes only the broader point: an idea becomes entrepreneurial when people take responsible action to pursue value under uncertainty.

collegeVersion.heading: Who can act entrepreneurially?
collegeVersion.body:
Entrepreneurship is often associated with a person who starts a company, and founders are an important example. But ownership is not a requirement in every serious definition. The OECD explicitly notes that entrepreneurial activity can occur within a business even when the people undertaking it do not own a stake in that company. A salaried team that develops and advances a genuinely new process, product, or market can therefore be engaging in entrepreneurial activity. OpenStax uses the term intrapreneur for an employee who applies creativity, vision, and risk-taking within a larger organization. The employee and employer do not bear the same personal exposure, but both can be involved in pursuing a new opportunity.

Likewise, entrepreneurship is not limited to for-profit corporations. OpenStax describes entrepreneurial ventures that may be businesses, organizations, projects, or operations, and notes that some focus on social needs through nonprofit forms. The organizational form changes legal obligations, governance, and funding; it does not settle whether the activity is entrepreneurial. This lesson is general education, not advice about choosing an entity, raising money, or accepting financial risk.

The role distinction matters in a case analysis. A founder who opens a familiar service using a proven local format is certainly a business owner and may be taking substantial personal risk. Whether to label the activity entrepreneurial depends on the definition being used and on whether it pursues a meaningful new product, process, market, or expansion. An employee who pushes a new process inside an established company may have no ownership at all but can still contribute entrepreneurial action. The useful question is not "Who deserves the label?" It is "What value-creating action is being pursued, what is new in this context, and what uncertainty does the actor have to manage?"

collegeVersion.heading: Entrepreneurship and small-business ownership overlap, but do not match
collegeVersion.body:
Small-business ownership and entrepreneurship often overlap, so a hard dividing line would be misleading. A person can both own a small business and pursue a new product, process, market, or expansion. A person can also buy or run an established small business skillfully without changing its basic model. The OECD cautions that entrepreneurship is not synonymous with small and medium-sized enterprises, startups, or self-employment; not every new business is necessarily entrepreneurial, and entrepreneurial activity is not confined to small firms.

Textbooks use different boundaries. One OpenStax text distinguishes entrepreneurs from owners who start or acquire an established model and intentionally remain small. Another acknowledges that small-business owners and franchisees can sometimes count as entrepreneurs, especially when they introduce something new to a region or market. These views are not a contradiction to memorize away. They show that the category has practical border cases. In a course, report, or policy discussion, state the definition before making the classification.

Do not use the distinction to rank people. Operating a stable, established business can require judgment, technical skill, customer care, and sustained work. Entrepreneurial action is a different analytical lens: it calls attention to pursuit of value through creation, expansion, or novelty under uncertainty. It is not a promise that a business will scale, a claim that owners of established firms lack initiative, or a license to ignore the ordinary obligations of running an organization.

vocabulary.definition: A person who pursues value by creating or expanding economic activity, often through a new product, process, or market.
Purposeful human action aimed at generating value through the creation or expansion of economic activity.
The broader phenomenon associated with entrepreneurial activity; it is not limited to one job title, firm size, or legal form.
A decision condition in which important future outcomes or their likelihoods are not fully known.
A risk taken after investigation and judgment intended to reduce avoidable exposure, not to eliminate uncertainty.
An employee who develops or advances entrepreneurial activity within an established organization rather than as its owner.
A person who owns, starts, or acquires a relatively small business; this role may overlap with entrepreneurship but is not identical to it.

eli10.simplifiedExplanation:
Entrepreneurship means trying to make something valuable happen when you cannot know exactly how it will turn out. A person might create a new service, improve how work gets done, or bring something useful to a place that did not have it before. The key is more than having an idea: someone has to do the work of pursuing it.

Being an entrepreneur does not mean being fearless or becoming rich. It means making choices when some answers are missing, learning from what happens, and being responsible for the effects of those choices. A person can do this while starting a company, working for a big company, or helping a nonprofit try a new approach.
eli10.analogy: Think of a community garden that has an unused patch of ground. An entrepreneurial team does not merely say, "Vegetables could grow there." It plans, gets permission, finds tools, chooses what to plant, and starts tending the plot. It hopes to create value—food, beauty, or a place for neighbors—but rain, pests, and participation are uncertain. The team can prepare, but it cannot control every result.
eli10.analogyLimits: A garden makes the work look more predictable than many entrepreneurial settings. Business and nonprofit ventures involve customers, money, rules, competitors, and ethical obligations that a garden analogy cannot fully capture. Also, not every entrepreneurial action creates a brand-new organization; it can improve or expand work inside one that already exists.

workedExample: A university dining department has recurring long lines at lunch. Jordan, a salaried operations coordinator, proposes a pre-order pickup lane using the department's existing app. Jordan maps the new workflow, asks the IT and kitchen teams to build a limited version, and sets a trial for one dining hall. The department does not know in advance whether enough students will use it, whether preparation times will hold, or whether the lane will reduce congestion. Jordan is not the owner of the university or the app, yet this is entrepreneurial activity: an employee is pursuing value through a new process under uncertainty. The later task is to learn from the trial and decide whether to revise, expand, or stop it—not to assume that the first idea must succeed.

commonMistakes.mistake: Equating entrepreneurship with having an idea.
commonMistakes.correction: An idea may be a starting point; entrepreneurship involves action to pursue value.

commonMistakes.mistake: Treating uncertainty as a reason to guess or ignore evidence.
commonMistakes.correction: Uncertainty cannot be eliminated, but investigation can reduce avoidable exposure and improve a decision.

commonMistakes.mistake: Assuming every startup or small business is entrepreneurial by definition.
commonMistakes.correction: Small businesses and startups can be entrepreneurial, but the classification depends on the definition and on the activity involved.

commonMistakes.mistake: Assuming only owners or founders can act entrepreneurially.
commonMistakes.correction: Employees can advance new products, processes, or markets within established organizations.

commonMistakes.mistake: Calling an outcome a success or failure proof of whether the activity was entrepreneurial.
commonMistakes.correction: Entrepreneurship concerns the pursuit of value; a venture can fail and still have involved entrepreneurial action.

compareContrast.distinction: The entrepreneur is a person; entrepreneurial activity is the value-seeking action that person or a team undertakes.
Risk concerns possible downside exposure that may sometimes be estimated; uncertainty includes important unknown outcomes or likelihoods.
They often overlap, but ownership is a role while entrepreneurship is an action-oriented phenomenon; neither implies the other in every case.

keyTakeaway: Entrepreneurship is value-seeking action under uncertainty, often through creating or expanding activity in a new way. It can occur in a startup, small business, nonprofit, or established organization, and it should not be confused with ownership, an idea alone, or a guaranteed outcome.

questionBank.prompt: Which statement best describes entrepreneurship in the OECD–Eurostat framing?
options: The phenomenon associated with action to generate value by creating or expanding economic activity.
A guarantee that a new company will earn a profit.
Any form of small-business ownership.
A personality trait limited to founders.
questionBank.explanation: The OECD–Eurostat framework centers entrepreneurship on value-seeking entrepreneurial activity. It does not promise profit, equate it with every small business, or limit it to founders.
questionBank.skill: Recall a source-grounded definition of entrepreneurship.

questionBank.prompt: Why is uncertainty central to entrepreneurial action?
options: It means research is unnecessary because outcomes cannot be known.
It proves that a decision will be risky in exactly the same way for everyone.
Important future outcomes or their likelihoods are not fully known when the action is taken.
It guarantees that a new product will be innovative.
questionBank.explanation: Entrepreneurial action proceeds before key outcomes are fully known. Research can reduce avoidable exposure, but it cannot make all future outcomes certain; uncertainty neither standardizes risk nor guarantees innovation.
questionBank.skill: Explain the role of uncertainty without confusing it with recklessness or certainty.

questionBank.prompt: A salaried employee leads a team that develops a new service process for an established company. The company has not decided whether it will scale the process. Which conclusion is best?
options: It cannot be entrepreneurial because the employee has no ownership stake.
It is automatically a small business because the process is new.
It is not entrepreneurial unless the process succeeds financially.
It can be entrepreneurial activity because new value-seeking action can occur inside an established organization.
questionBank.explanation: The OECD notes that entrepreneurial activity can occur within firms without an ownership stake, and OpenStax describes intrapreneurs in larger organizations. A small-business label and financial success are not requirements.
questionBank.skill: Apply the ownership distinction to an organizational scenario.

questionBank.prompt: Which comparison between entrepreneurship and small-business ownership is most accurate?
options: They are identical because all small businesses are new.
They never overlap because entrepreneurship only happens in large companies.
They may overlap, but ownership is not itself proof of entrepreneurial activity and entrepreneurship is not confined to small firms.
Small-business ownership becomes entrepreneurship only after a firm has grown past a fixed number of employees.
questionBank.explanation: The two categories can overlap, but OECD guidance says entrepreneurship is not synonymous with SMEs, startups, or self-employment. No fixed employee threshold makes the distinction.
questionBank.skill: Distinguish overlapping categories without imposing a false binary.

questionBank.prompt: Which action best shows calculated risk rather than reckless certainty?
options: Committing all available funds because confidence is high.
Gathering relevant information, limiting an initial commitment, and revising after results while accepting that uncertainty remains.
Waiting until every future outcome is known before acting.
Assuming a past success guarantees the same result in a new market.
questionBank.explanation: Calculated risk uses investigation and judgment to reduce avoidable exposure while recognizing that uncertainty remains. The other choices either ignore evidence, demand impossible certainty, or treat a past result as a guarantee.
questionBank.skill: Identify responsible action under uncertainty.

title: Finding Business Ideas
in30Seconds: Finding a business idea is a disciplined search for possible ways to create value, not a hunt for one brilliant flash. Start by noticing friction, waste, underused assets, or changing conditions. Then turn observations into several candidate concepts and apply a quick screen: who might benefit, what alternatives exist, what resources would be needed, and what constraints apply. A promising idea is still a hypothesis, not a business yet.
whyItMatters: Idea generation gives entrepreneurship a repeatable starting point. It helps students move beyond copying a fashionable app or assuming that a personal preference is automatically a market. Combining observation with public context data and a basic feasibility screen can reveal better questions before time or money is committed. It also establishes an ethical habit: do not build a concept on avoidable privacy harms, misleading claims, or disregard for the people affected by it.
learningObjectives: Explain why a business idea and a viable opportunity are different.
Apply observation, recombination, and context scanning to generate candidate ideas.
Distinguish market-context evidence from proof that a specific offer will succeed.
Use a preliminary feasibility screen to compare candidate ideas.
Evaluate ethical boundaries involving data collection and future marketing claims.

collegeVersion.heading: Generate a portfolio, not a single answer
collegeVersion.body:
A business idea is a proposed way to create and deliver value. It can begin with a personal annoyance, an underused asset, a change in technology, a policy shift, a new distribution channel, or a different combination of familiar elements. That breadth matters because an idea is not yet an entrepreneurial opportunity. OpenStax frames opportunity as the meeting of identifiable demand and the feasibility of providing a product or service. The practical implication is modest but useful: generate more than one candidate before becoming attached to any one of them.

Three methods help make the search deliberate. First, observe routines. Watch for repeated workarounds, waiting, handoffs, information gaps, unused capacity, and waste. Record the setting, the actors, the current workaround, and the constraint; this is evidence for an idea queue, not proof of a market. Second, recombine. Ask whether an existing capability, channel, or asset could be applied in a different setting. A campus print shop, for example, might bundle late-night pickup with preformatted course-packet ordering; neither element is novel, but their combination may be useful. Third, scan changes in context. New tools, demographic shifts, local infrastructure, regulation, prices, or work patterns can change what is practical. Context is an input to creative search, not a prediction machine.

A useful output is an idea card: a short name, the observed situation, the proposed change, the likely beneficiary, existing alternatives, major assumptions, and known constraints. Keep the language conditional. Writing “could reduce a handoff” is more honest and more actionable than writing “customers need this.” The latter belongs to later problem identification and customer discovery work.

collegeVersion.heading: Use public context and competitors as clues
collegeVersion.body:
Secondary research is information already published by someone else. It is well suited to broad, measurable context: the size and composition of a local population, employment patterns, the number of establishments in an industry, or changes in consumer spending. In the United States, Census Business Builder lets users examine selected demographic, economic, and business data by business type and location. The SBA likewise points founders to demographic, economic, location, saturation, and pricing questions when they study a market. These sources can help a student ask a sharper question, such as whether a particular area has enough potential users or many incumbent providers. They cannot establish that a particular offer will be adopted.

Competitive scanning is also idea generation, not merely a later defense exercise. List direct alternatives, indirect alternatives, and the non-purchase option: what people do when they buy nothing. Study how alternatives package the task, what is inconvenient about their delivery, where their coverage ends, and which constraints seem to shape their choices. The goal is not to declare competitors weak. It is to spot a specific difference worth investigating: a neglected segment, a difficult time of day, an awkward process, unused capacity, or a clearer way to assemble services. Do not copy protected branding, proprietary content, or another firm’s confidential material.

Trend scanning needs the same restraint. A rising statistic may suggest a place to look, but it does not prove a durable opportunity. Check the geography, period, definition, and source behind a trend. Ask what alternative explanation could produce the pattern. Treat public data as a map: it narrows the terrain but does not tell you exactly where to build.

collegeVersion.heading: Screen early, revise cheaply, and set ethical limits
collegeVersion.body:
An early feasibility screen compares candidates before substantial commitment. It is not a forecast and it does not replace later research. For each idea, assess four dimensions. First, potential value: is there a clear task, outcome, or access improvement the concept might provide? Second, context and alternatives: is there enough evidence that the relevant setting, segment, and competitive landscape deserve further study? Third, execution: what skills, partners, inputs, technology, distribution, time, and cash would be required? Fourth, constraints: what safety, accessibility, legal, environmental, operational, or reputational issues could block or reshape the idea? OpenStax identifies demand, market structure and size, and margins and resources as basic concerns in opportunity screening; a student screen can use those concerns without pretending to calculate a precise probability of success.

Score each dimension with brief evidence notes rather than a single impressive-looking total. An idea can be promising but currently infeasible because a required capability is unavailable. That is a useful result: revise the concept, narrow its scope, seek a different channel, or park it. Kill criteria are equally useful. For example, a team might discard any concept that depends on data it cannot justify collecting, a claim it cannot substantiate, or an unmanageable regulatory requirement.

Ethics belongs before launch. If a concept requires personal information, collect only what is necessary for a legitimate purpose, protect it, and do not retain it indefinitely; FTC guidance provides that U.S.-specific baseline. If the concept later makes advertising claims in the United States, those claims must be truthful, non-deceptive, fair, and evidence-based under FTC guidance. Other countries and regulated categories may impose different or additional requirements. These are guardrails, not a substitute for qualified local legal or privacy advice. A durable idea-generation practice therefore produces options while refusing to normalize avoidable harm.

vocabulary.definition: A preliminary proposal for creating and delivering value through a product, service, process, or venture.
A situation in which identifiable demand can plausibly be met by a feasible offering.
Systematically noticing actions, workarounds, constraints, or unused resources in a real setting.
Creating a candidate concept by applying familiar capabilities, assets, or channels in a new combination.
Analysis of data or information that has already been collected and published by another source.
The direct, indirect, and non-purchase alternatives available to a potential user in a particular setting.
A preliminary comparison of candidate concepts using explicit criteria such as context, resources, alternatives, and constraints.
Limiting personal information collection and retention to what is necessary for a legitimate purpose.

eli10.simplifiedExplanation: Finding business ideas is like keeping a notebook of little puzzles you notice. Maybe a line is always slow, a tool sits unused, or people keep inventing the same workaround. Write down several puzzles and several possible fixes. Then ask: could this fix actually be made, what else do people use, and would it create a new problem? You are not choosing a winner yet; you are choosing which ideas deserve a closer look.
eli10.analogy: Imagine searching for a good place to plant a garden. You look for more than a pretty patch of ground: sunlight, water, soil, space, and what is already growing nearby all matter. An idea is a seed; the surrounding conditions help decide which seeds are worth testing.
eli10.analogyLimits: Businesses involve people, consent, money, rules, and competing choices, so they cannot be evaluated as simply as a garden plot. A favorable screen does not guarantee that anyone will choose the offer.

workedExample: Hypothetical example: A student notices that campus-club officers repeatedly pass spreadsheets, receipts, and approval messages among several volunteers. She creates three idea cards: a receipt-organizing service, a shared approval dashboard, and a training kit for treasurers. She scans public campus information and alternatives already used by student groups, then applies a four-part screen. The dashboard may offer value, but it would require security review and access to financial information. The training kit has lower privacy risk and can be delivered with existing skills, but similar materials already exist. The receipt service may require accounting expertise and data handling practices the student does not have. The screen does not choose a business; it makes the next question clearer: which concept can be refined without collecting unjustified personal financial data?

commonMistakes.mistake: Treating a clever concept as proof of an opportunity.
commonMistakes.correction: Keep it as a candidate until its context, alternatives, resources, and constraints have been examined.

commonMistakes.mistake: Using a broad trend as if it proves demand for one exact offer.
commonMistakes.correction: Use the trend to focus exploration, then distinguish broad context from evidence about a particular offer.

commonMistakes.mistake: Calling competitors irrelevant because the idea has a new feature.
commonMistakes.correction: Include direct, indirect, and non-purchase alternatives when scanning the landscape.

commonMistakes.mistake: Collecting personal data simply because it might be useful later.
commonMistakes.correction: Define a legitimate purpose, minimize collection and retention, and protect any data collected.

commonMistakes.mistake: Making future marketing promises before evidence exists.
commonMistakes.correction: Plan only claims that can be truthful, non-deceptive, fair, and evidence-based in the applicable jurisdiction.

compareContrast.distinction: An idea is a preliminary proposal; an opportunity has enough indication of demand and feasibility to merit further development.
Published data supplies broad context; it does not by itself establish that a particular offer will be chosen.
Scanning studies alternatives and gaps; copying may ignore ethics, intellectual-property boundaries, and meaningful differentiation.

keyTakeaway: Strong business ideas come from disciplined observation, recombination, and context scanning, then earn further attention through an early feasibility and ethics screen. A screen prioritizes what to investigate; it never guarantees a business outcome.

questionBank.prompt: Which statement best distinguishes a business idea from an entrepreneurial opportunity?
options: An idea is a preliminary proposal, while an opportunity also requires plausible demand and feasibility.
An idea must be a physical product, while an opportunity must be a service.
An idea is always local, while an opportunity is always global.
An idea is private, while an opportunity is protected by a patent.
questionBank.explanation: A is correct because feasibility and identifiable demand must be considered before an idea is treated as an opportunity. B, C, and D invent distinctions that do not define the terms.
questionBank.skill: distinguishing an idea from an opportunity

questionBank.prompt: A student uses Census Business Builder to compare age distribution, income, and existing business data across two neighborhoods. What is the most accurate use of this information?
options: It proves that residents will buy the student's proposed service.
It provides context that can help focus which setting deserves further exploration.
It replaces the need to consider competitors or resources.
It guarantees that one neighborhood has an unsatisfied market.
questionBank.explanation: B is correct: public demographic and business data support contextual scanning. A and D overclaim what the data prove, and C wrongly treats data as a substitute for screening alternatives and execution.
questionBank.skill: using public context data with appropriate limits

questionBank.prompt: Which item belongs most directly in an early feasibility screen?
options: A guaranteed five-year revenue forecast
A promise that no competitor will respond
The skills, inputs, and distribution needed to make the concept work
A final decision on every future price
questionBank.explanation: C is correct because feasibility screening considers resources and execution requirements. A and B claim certainty that a screen cannot provide; D is a later operating decision, not a basic screening criterion.
questionBank.skill: identifying feasibility criteria

questionBank.prompt: A team wants to build a tool that stores every visitor's contact details indefinitely in case they become useful. Which response best follows the lesson's ethical boundary?
options: Collect all available information because more data always improves ideas.
Keep the data only if the team promises never to look at it.
Publish the data so other entrepreneurs can learn from it.
Define a legitimate purpose, collect only what is necessary, protect it, and avoid retaining it longer than needed.
questionBank.explanation: D matches the FTC-aligned data-minimization boundary. A ignores necessity, B does not address collection or protection, and C creates an additional privacy risk.
questionBank.skill: applying data-minimization principles

questionBank.prompt: Why should a founder include the non-purchase option when scanning alternatives?
options: People may solve the task by doing nothing or using a workaround, which can reveal the real alternatives.
Non-purchase options are illegal in most markets.
It makes market data unnecessary.
It proves a new feature will be successful.
questionBank.explanation: A is correct because doing nothing or using a workaround competes with a proposed offer. B is false, while C and D make unsupported claims about evidence and success.
questionBank.skill: analyzing the competitive landscape

title: Problem Identification
in30Seconds: Problem identification turns a vague complaint into a bounded, testable description of a customer’s situation. An entrepreneur asks who has the problem, when it occurs, what gets in the way, and what consequence follows. A complaint or a decline in sales may be a useful signal, but it is not automatically the cause. Treat early explanations as hypotheses, then use appropriate evidence to decide whether to revise, narrow, or reject them.
whyItMatters: A venture can build a polished solution for a problem that is too vague, affects the wrong group, or has been misdiagnosed. Clear problem identification makes later work more disciplined: it gives customer discovery and market research a focused question, helps separate evidence from assumptions, and prevents a team from mistaking a preferred product for a demonstrated need. The skill also transfers beyond startups, because it is a way to reason carefully before committing resources to an explanation or response.
learningObjectives: Define problem identification as a bounded description of a customer context and an unmet need or harmful gap.
Distinguish an observable symptom from a plausible underlying cause.
Frame a problem hypothesis that identifies a customer, situation, consequence, and assumption to check.
Analyze what a piece of evidence can support and what it cannot establish.
Apply problem framing to revise an overly broad entrepreneurial claim.

collegeVersion.heading: A problem is a gap in a particular context
collegeVersion.body:
In entrepreneurship, problem identification is the work of describing an important gap before proposing a remedy. The gap is between a present condition and a desired condition for a particular customer or user. OpenStax describes clarification as recognizing the gap between the current and desired states, including a gap between customer or social needs and actual circumstances. That idea matters because the phrase “people need a better app” is not yet a problem definition. It does not say which people, what they are trying to do, or what “better” means.

A usable problem description sets boundaries. Name the affected group, the situation or task, the obstacle, and the consequence. For example: “Independent tutors who schedule several weekly sessions lose time reconciling changes made by families in separate text-message threads, leading to missed updates and duplicate follow-up.” This statement does not claim that a calendar application will solve the issue. It identifies a setting in which a burden may exist. Its boundaries make it possible to investigate the claim rather than defend a favorite solution.

collegeVersion.heading: Symptoms are signals, not explanations
collegeVersion.body:
A symptom is an observable result or warning sign: abandoned carts, late deliveries, repeat support requests, or falling renewal rates. It can show that something deserves attention, but it does not by itself identify why it happened. The same symptom may arise from different mechanisms. If customers abandon an online checkout, possible contributors could include an unexpected delivery charge, a payment error, a confusing form, a requirement to create an account, or a mismatch between the offer and the customer’s intent. Choosing one cause because it is convenient turns a signal into an unsupported story.

Looking beneath a symptom does not mean pretending that every problem has one hidden, permanent root cause. AHRQ’s systems-oriented discussion of root-cause analysis emphasizes underlying and contributing factors rather than stopping at an individual mistake. In a business context, the useful transfer is modest: ask what conditions and steps could plausibly produce the observed result, and be ready for more than one contributing factor. The goal here is not to run a formal safety investigation. It is to avoid designing a solution for the first explanation that comes to mind.

collegeVersion.heading: Turn an explanation into a problem hypothesis
collegeVersion.body:
A problem hypothesis is a provisional claim that can be checked. One practical form is: “We believe [a defined group] experiences [a concrete obstacle] when [a situation occurs], which leads to [a meaningful consequence], because [a proposed condition or cause].” The bracketed cause is deliberately an assumption, not a conclusion. In the tutor example, a team might hypothesize that the trouble comes from families using several channels without a shared change record. Another plausible explanation is that scheduling policies are unclear. These are competing explanations, so the team should not present either as settled fact.

This framing keeps a problem statement separate from a solution pitch. “Tutors need our all-in-one scheduling platform” contains a solution and offers no evidence that the platform addresses the burden. “Tutors lose track of schedule changes across separate channels” is a claim about a situation; a later investigation can ask how frequent, costly, and widespread it is, and whether existing alternatives already handle it adequately. The U.S. Small Business Administration similarly directs market research toward questions about demand, market size, location, saturation, and what potential customers pay for alternatives. Those questions test the context around a proposed problem; they do not make the problem true merely by being asked.

collegeVersion.heading: Use evidence at the strength it can bear
collegeVersion.body:
Evidence should be matched to the claim. A public data source can describe population, income, employment, or industry conditions, but it may be too broad to establish a niche customer’s workflow. The SBA notes that existing sources can efficiently answer general, quantitative questions but may not be specific to an audience, while direct research can yield more nuanced information about a particular business or customer. Thus, a local demographic count can support a claim about the size or characteristics of a place; it cannot prove that every person there feels a particular frustration.

Likewise, a few observations can produce a useful hypothesis but cannot establish prevalence or causation. A team should record what it saw, what it inferred, and what remains unknown. It can then state a narrow next question, such as whether the scheduling burden recurs across tutors who use different coordination systems. This lesson does not prescribe interview technique or a sampling plan; those belong to customer-interview and market-research work. The central habit is intellectual honesty: revise the problem definition when evidence points to another segment, context, severity, or contributing factor. A well-framed problem is not a promise of a business opportunity. It is a clearer question for subsequent investigation.

vocabulary.definition: The process of describing a specific gap, obstacle, or unmet need in a defined customer context before choosing a solution.
The circumstances in which a particular group is trying to complete a task or make a decision, including relevant constraints and alternatives.
An observable result or warning sign that suggests a problem may exist but does not, by itself, establish its cause.
A condition or action that may help produce an observed outcome without necessarily being the only cause.
A provisional, checkable claim about who experiences an obstacle, when it occurs, and what consequence it has.
A boundary on what particular information can reasonably support, such as a limit on specificity, representativeness, or causal inference.

eli10.simplifiedExplanation: Suppose a school hallway is always crowded after lunch. “The hallway is crowded” is a useful clue, but it does not tell you what to change. Maybe one door is locked, two classes end at the same time, or students stop at a water fountain in the middle. Each possibility needs checking. In a business, “customers leave the website” works the same way: it is a clue, not the whole answer. It tells you where to look next, not which answer must be right.
eli10.analogy: Problem identification is like a doctor writing down the symptoms, when they happen, and who has them before choosing a treatment. The notes help the doctor test explanations instead of handing out medicine based on one guess.
eli10.analogyLimits: Businesses are not medical clinics, and customer problems often involve preferences, trade-offs, and changing alternatives rather than a diagnosis with one correct treatment. The analogy is only about starting with careful observation and keeping explanations provisional.

workedExample: A student notices that several classmates complain about missing changes to group-project meetings. Her first statement is, “Students need a better group-work app.” That jumps to a solution and treats complaints as proof. She reframes the issue: “Students in large, multi-course project teams may miss schedule changes when updates are split among email, chat, and course platforms, causing wasted trips or delayed work.” The phrase “may” marks a hypothesis. Missed meetings are the symptom; split update channels are a possible contributing factor. The student could later learn that the main issue is instead unclear team roles, low notification use, or a school policy. Public enrollment data could show how many potential users are present, but it could not show why these particular students missed changes. The next work is to gather evidence that can distinguish among these explanations, not to declare an app validated.

commonMistakes.mistake: Naming a product as the problem.
commonMistakes.correction: Describe the customer’s situation and consequence before proposing a product, feature, or channel.

commonMistakes.mistake: Treating one complaint or metric change as proof of a cause.
commonMistakes.correction: Use it as a signal, list plausible explanations, and label the preferred explanation as a hypothesis.

commonMistakes.mistake: Writing for everyone.
commonMistakes.correction: Specify the group and situation so that the claim can be investigated and later revised.

commonMistakes.mistake: Using broad statistics to prove a narrow experience.
commonMistakes.correction: Use broad data for broad claims and seek more specific evidence for claims about a particular context.

compareContrast.distinction: A symptom is an observable outcome; a contributing factor is a proposed condition that may help explain that outcome and requires support.
A hypothesis is deliberately provisional and testable; a conclusion is warranted only after sufficient evidence for the stated claim.
Context describes the situation in which a burden occurs; market size estimates how many potential customers may be in scope.

keyTakeaway: A strong entrepreneurial problem statement specifies a customer context and a harmful gap without smuggling in a solution. Symptoms and early observations are evidence to investigate, not permission to assume a single cause or a validated opportunity.

title: Customer Discovery
in30Seconds: Customer discovery is a disciplined way to test what you think you know about a particular group of people and the problem they face. Begin with assumptions, seek evidence that could change them, and decide what to learn next. It is not a vote on whether people like an idea, a shortcut to proving demand, or the same thing as building a solution.
whyItMatters: Early business ideas often combine facts, guesses, and hopes. Customer discovery gives students a way to separate them. It connects a claimed customer problem to a defined segment, evidence, and a next decision, which makes later work on market research, interviews, value propositions, and products more precise. The method is useful beyond startups: a campus office, nonprofit, or established firm can use it before committing scarce time, money, or attention. It reduces avoidable overconfidence but cannot guarantee adoption, revenue, or success.
learningObjectives: Define customer discovery as a process for testing problem-and-segment assumptions.
Distinguish an assumption, a hypothesis, an observation, and a conclusion.
Frame a discovery hypothesis so that evidence could change the next decision.
Explain how a learning loop updates or retires an assumption.
Evaluate why early evidence is directional rather than proof of a market.

collegeVersion.heading: Discovery tests an assumption, not a solution pitch
collegeVersion.body:
Customer discovery is the early inquiry that asks whether a specified group appears to experience a specified situation strongly enough to deserve further investigation. It is helpful to treat the phrase as an operating definition rather than a promise embedded in startup vocabulary. The object of inquiry is not an abstract "customer" and not a finished offering. It is an assumption linking a segment, a circumstance, and a possible problem. For example: "Commuter students who arrive on campus after work have difficulty obtaining a reliable evening meal between class and closing time." The statement may be plausible, but it is still an assumption until evidence bears on it.

This focus sets a boundary around nearby topics. Problem identification asks what is happening and what may contribute to it. Customer discovery asks whether the proposed problem occurs for a defined group and under what conditions. Customer interviews are one possible way of gathering direct evidence, but their recruiting, consent, prompts, and facilitation belong to a separate skill set. Value proposition work asks how an organization might address a supported need; discovery should not quietly turn into asking people to approve a proposed answer. Similarly, market research examines broader demand, size, competitors, and conditions. Discovery can use those inputs, but it stays close to an uncertainty that affects the next entrepreneurial decision.

The SBA describes market research as bringing together consumer behavior and economic trends to improve an idea. It also distinguishes existing information from direct research. Existing information is often useful for broad, quantitative questions such as demographics, incomes, industry trends, or market conditions. Direct inquiry can add detail about a particular audience or context, although it takes time and resources. In discovery, that contrast prevents a false choice: a team can examine available context and then seek focused evidence about the assumption that remains uncertain.

collegeVersion.heading: From a claim to a learning loop
collegeVersion.body:
A usable discovery hypothesis is specific enough that different observations would lead to different interpretations. A simple structure is: for [defined segment], in [particular situation], [problem or behavior] occurs because [proposed condition]; if that is true, we expect to observe [evidence]. This does not require pretending to know the cause with certainty. The proposed condition is a part of the hypothesis that might need revision. The expected evidence should be observable and relevant to the decision, such as repeated accounts of a workaround, records showing a pattern at a relevant time, or a mismatch between available options and stated constraints.

A learning loop has four connected moves. First, name the assumption and the decision it informs. Second, identify the most important uncertainty and formulate a hypothesis. Third, gather and organize evidence that speaks to that hypothesis, using sources that fit the question. Fourth, interpret the evidence against the original assumption and choose a next move: retain the assumption provisionally, revise it, narrow the segment, investigate a competing explanation, or stop pursuing that line. The word provisionally matters. Retaining an assumption means it has survived the evidence so far; it does not mean it has been proven.

Research goals keep the loop from becoming collection for its own sake. OpenStax describes primary research as collecting new data to answer a specific question or questions, and its market-research discussion emphasizes gathering and analyzing target-market information. A team should therefore write what decision the evidence can change before treating information as useful. If the current decision is whether evening access deserves further study, evidence about a broad national food trend may supply context but may not resolve the local access assumption. Conversely, a few local observations may illuminate context but cannot establish the size of a wider market. The appropriate evidence depends on the claim being tested.

collegeVersion.heading: What early evidence can and cannot establish
collegeVersion.body:
Customer discovery produces evidence, not a verdict from the market. A small number of observations may reveal a pattern worth investigating, contradict an assumption, or expose a missing segment boundary. They do not by themselves show how common a problem is, how many people would pay, whether a new offering will work, or whether a venture will succeed. People who are easy to reach may differ from people the organization ultimately hopes to serve. Memory, context, incentives, and the wording of a research activity can also shape what is observed. These are reasons to record limits, not reasons to ignore early learning.

Triangulation is a practical safeguard: compare more than one relevant form of evidence and look for convergence as well as disagreement. A discovery team might compare public location or demographic information, operational records, and direct accounts of the setting. Disagreement is informative. If broad data suggest that many people could be in a segment but local observations show a different constraint, the team should investigate the mismatch rather than average it away. SBA guidance lists demand, market size, economic indicators, location, saturation, and alternative prices as distinct market questions. One type of evidence rarely answers all of them.

Good discovery documentation separates observations from interpretations. "The dining hall closes at 7 p.m." is an observation if verified. "Commuter students lack a workable dinner option" is an interpretation that needs supporting evidence and a defined scope. "They will buy a meal subscription" is a further prediction, not something established merely by showing an access issue. Keeping these levels separate makes it easier to hand off work to later topics: customer-interview practice can deepen direct inquiry; market research can estimate broader context; value-proposition work can formulate an answer. Customer discovery has done its job when it makes the next uncertainty and the next decision clearer.

vocabulary.definition: A structured process for testing assumptions about a defined group, its situation, and a possible problem before treating those assumptions as settled.
A bounded group of people or organizations that shares characteristics relevant to the question being investigated.
A statement accepted provisionally for planning or inquiry but not yet adequately supported for the decision at hand.
A specific, testable proposed explanation or expectation that evidence could support, complicate, or contradict.
A recorded fact, behavior, account, or measurement gathered through an identified source or method.
A recurring sequence of naming an uncertainty, gathering relevant evidence, interpreting it, and updating the next decision.
Comparing multiple relevant sources or forms of evidence to check where they converge, differ, or leave uncertainty.

eli10.simplifiedExplanation:
Customer discovery is like checking whether a problem is real for a particular group before spending a lot of effort trying to fix it. First, write down what you think is happening. Then look for information that might show you are right, partly right, or wrong. If the information changes the picture, change your next step too.

A few people describing the same difficulty can be a useful clue. It is not a magic stamp that says every person has the problem or that a new business will work. The clue tells you what to investigate next. Careful discovery keeps the clue, the guess, and the conclusion in separate boxes.
eli10.analogy: Imagine a detective trying to understand why a school library is empty after lunch. The detective does not decide the answer after seeing one empty table. They write a possible explanation, compare the schedule, room hours, and what students report, then revise the explanation when the pieces do not fit. Customer discovery works similarly: it investigates a focused uncertainty before committing to an answer.
eli10.analogyLimits: A customer-discovery team is not solving a crime or trying to prove one final cause. People can have different needs in different situations, and business decisions also involve resources, alternatives, and ethics. The analogy also does not mean that a team should use investigative pressure; participation and information handling require care.

workedExample: A campus team is considering whether evening students need a food-access improvement. Its initial assumption is that students who arrive after work cannot get a practical meal between a 6:00 p.m. class and the end of the evening. The team first checks posted dining hours and a campus schedule, then reviews how many courses meet in that time window. Those sources show a possible access gap but not whether the students experience it as a serious problem. The team records the remaining uncertainty: which commuters are affected, on which days, and what workarounds they already use. It then gathers focused direct evidence and compares it with the timetable. Several students report bringing food from home, but others leave campus early because they prefer that routine. The team revises the assumption from "evening students need a meal service" to "some commuters with back-to-back evening commitments may lack a workable food option." The next decision is to investigate that narrower situation, not to launch a subscription or declare demand proven.

commonMistakes.mistake: Starting with a favorite solution and treating every finding as support for it.
commonMistakes.correction: State the segment-and-problem assumption first and allow evidence to revise or retire it before developing an answer.

commonMistakes.mistake: Calling a broad demographic statistic proof that a local group has a particular problem.
commonMistakes.correction: Use broad data for context and seek evidence that bears on the specific segment, situation, and claim.

commonMistakes.mistake: Treating a few early observations as a market-size estimate or revenue forecast.
commonMistakes.correction: Describe early evidence as directional; estimating prevalence or demand requires methods suited to those claims.

commonMistakes.mistake: Collecting interesting information without naming the decision it could change.
commonMistakes.correction: Connect each inquiry to an uncertainty and a next decision in the learning loop.

compareContrast.distinction: Discovery is the broader process of testing assumptions and updating decisions; interviews are one possible direct-research method whose mechanics are a separate topic.
An observation records what a source shows or reports; a conclusion is an interpretation that should be limited by the evidence.
Discovery investigates whether a segment-and-problem assumption warrants further work; a value proposition frames a proposed answer and its benefit.

keyTakeaway: Customer discovery turns a segment-and-problem guess into a learning process: state what must be true, seek evidence that could change the next decision, and record what remains uncertain. Its result is better-grounded next steps, not proof that a market or solution will succeed.

questionBank.prompt: Which statement best defines customer discovery in this lesson?
options: A process for testing assumptions about a defined group and a possible problem.
A method for persuading people to approve a finished solution.
A calculation that determines market size from one observation.
A guarantee that a business idea will succeed.
questionBank.explanation: Customer discovery tests problem-and-segment assumptions. It does not ask for approval of a finished solution, calculate a market from one observation, or guarantee a result.
questionBank.skill: Recall the purpose and boundary of customer discovery.

questionBank.prompt: Which item is a hypothesis rather than an observation or a conclusion?
options: The dining hall's posted closing time is 7 p.m.
Commuter students with back-to-back evening commitments are likely to report difficulty obtaining a practical meal on campus.
The available evidence proves that all evening students need a meal subscription.
Six students reported bringing food from home.
questionBank.explanation: The second option makes a specific expectation that evidence can test. Posted hours and reported behavior are observations, while the claim about all students and a subscription exceeds the evidence.
questionBank.skill: Distinguish a testable hypothesis from observations and overbroad conclusions.

questionBank.prompt: A team finds that several reachable users describe a recurring workaround, but the team has not studied how common the situation is. What is the most justified conclusion?
options: The workaround proves that most potential customers will pay for a new product.
The team should ignore the finding because it is not a population estimate.
The finding is directional evidence worth investigating further, with its limits recorded.
The finding establishes the exact market size.
questionBank.explanation: A small early finding can challenge or support an assumption enough to guide the next inquiry, but it cannot establish prevalence, market size, willingness to pay, or success.
questionBank.skill: Apply evidence limits to an early discovery finding.

questionBank.prompt: Which sequence best represents a customer-discovery learning loop?
options: Choose a solution, promote it, and treat positive comments as validation.
Collect every available data point, then decide what question mattered.
Estimate revenue, write a value proposition, and skip contradictory evidence.
Name an assumption and decision, form a testable hypothesis, gather relevant evidence, then update the next move.
questionBank.explanation: A learning loop begins with a decision-relevant uncertainty and uses evidence to retain provisionally, revise, narrow, investigate further, or stop an assumption. The other sequences embed confirmation bias or reverse the inquiry.
questionBank.skill: Analyze the order and purpose of a learning loop.

questionBank.prompt: Why might a team compare public demographic information with focused direct evidence about a local setting?
options: The sources can answer different parts of the question and reveal where the evidence converges or conflicts.
Public data automatically make direct evidence unnecessary.
Direct evidence can always replace any need for broader context.
If the sources differ, the team should discard both without further inquiry.
questionBank.explanation: Broad existing information can provide context, while focused direct evidence can illuminate a specific audience or setting. Comparing them can show agreement, disagreement, and the next uncertainty; neither source type automatically settles every claim.
questionBank.skill: Choose complementary evidence for a bounded discovery question.

title: Customer Interviews
in30Seconds: Customer interviews are planned conversations with people who have relevant experience of a task, problem, or decision. They help a team learn how people describe what they actually do, what gets in the way, and what context matters. The method is exploratory: a small, deliberately chosen set of interviews can uncover patterns and sharpen questions, but it cannot tell you how common a view is across a whole market.
whyItMatters: Interviews can keep an entrepreneurial team close to real experiences instead of its own assumptions. Done well, they produce better questions, expose differences between participants, and reveal where a workflow or language is misunderstood. Done carelessly, they can pressure people, collect unnecessary personal data, or turn a polite reaction into false proof of demand. The transferable skill is disciplined listening: obtain voluntary participation, ask about concrete past behavior, preserve the difference between an observation and an interpretation, and report the limits of what a small qualitative sample can support.
learningObjectives: Define a customer interview and explain its exploratory evidence limit.
Plan an interview round around a specific learning question and relevant participant criteria.
Distinguish open, neutral questions from leading, hypothetical, or solution-pitch questions.
Apply listening and follow-up techniques that seek concrete examples without putting words in a participant's mouth.
Explain how consent, privacy, and careful note analysis protect participants and improve the quality of findings.

collegeVersion.heading: What an interview can—and cannot—tell you
collegeVersion.body:
A customer interview is a structured conversation used to learn from someone with relevant experience. For an entrepreneurial team, its value is usually depth and context: what the person was trying to do, what happened, what alternatives they considered, what language they use, and which conditions changed the experience. The interview is not a sales call disguised as research, and it is not a referendum on whether a team likes its own idea. A participant may be a current user of an existing process, a likely user of a proposed service, or another person who directly experiences the workflow the team needs to understand. The selection must follow the learning question. If the question concerns how independent tutors manage schedule changes, interviewing people who merely know a tutor is weaker evidence than interviewing tutors who coordinate recurring sessions.

A useful interview round begins with one or two decisions the team needs to inform and a short discussion guide. The guide gives every participant a comparable core set of topics, while leaving room to pursue a relevant detail. GOV.UK's guidance on in-depth interviews recommends open, neutral questions and attention to stories and real examples. That is why a prompt such as “Tell me about the last time a schedule changed” is often more informative than “Would you use our schedule-change app?” The first asks for a remembered event; the second introduces a proposed answer and invites courtesy, imagination, or a quick yes.

Interview evidence is qualitative and exploratory. A small set of deliberately recruited participants can surface recurring patterns, contrast situations, and generate a better next question. It does not calculate a population percentage, establish a market size, or prove that a particular product will sell. GOV.UK contrasts small rounds commonly used for interviews with survey-style methods that need much larger samples for clear quantitative findings. The precise number appropriate for an interview round depends on the question, heterogeneity of the people involved, access constraints, and what has already been learned. Rather than borrow a magic number, state who was interviewed, why they were relevant, what differences were included or missed, and what the sample cannot represent. Market sizing and statistically representative research require their own design.

collegeVersion.heading: Plan recruitment and questions without steering the answer
collegeVersion.body:
Recruitment is part of the method, not an administrative afterthought. Write inclusion criteria that connect to the behavior or situation under study: for example, tutors who independently schedule at least several recurring sessions, or families who recently changed a session. Deliberately seek meaningful variation when it could change the experience—such as a new versus experienced tutor, a different scheduling arrangement, a disability or access need, or a different tool setup. This is not a claim of statistical representativeness. It is a way to avoid letting the most convenient or enthusiastic contacts stand in for everyone. Record the recruiting route and likely sources of bias. Friends, early supporters, and people recruited from a founder's network may be useful to learn from, but their relationship to the project can shape what they say.

Use a guide with an opening, a small number of topic areas, and a closing. Begin by explaining the purpose in plain language and confirming consent; then ask broad questions before narrower ones. Open questions commonly start with “how,” “what,” “tell me about,” or “walk me through.” Neutral wording does not contain the preferred conclusion. Compare “What happened when you needed to reschedule?” with “How frustrating was it when the confusing system made you reschedule?” The second question assumes both that the system was confusing and that frustration occurred. It pressures the participant to agree with the interviewer’s framing. Avoid stacking two questions together as well: “How do you schedule and pay and communicate?” gives no clear answer target.

Questions about an actual episode are usually more useful than questions about a hypothetical future purchase. “What did you do next?” “What else did you try?” and “What made that option workable or not?” can expose constraints, workarounds, and alternatives. A participant's claim that they would buy something is still a statement about a possible future, not evidence that they will do so. The point is not to catch people being wrong. It is to understand their present practice before treating a solution as the center of the conversation. This lesson therefore does not build a customer-discovery framework or teach a final value proposition; it teaches the interview craft that can supply bounded evidence to those later activities.

collegeVersion.heading: Listen, record, and analyze with care
collegeVersion.body:
Good moderation makes the participant, not the interviewer, do most of the explaining. Listen for the sequence of a real event: trigger, goal, actions, tools, obstacles, choices, and outcome. Pause rather than filling silence with an answer. A brief reflection can check understanding—“It sounds as if the text message was easy to miss because you were teaching”—but frame it as a check, not a correction. Then ask a simple, non-leading follow-up: “Can you tell me more about what happened after that?” or “What made that difficult?” Follow the participant's relevant detail while returning gently to the guide when needed. Do not debate, promise a solution, or treat a participant’s politeness as approval.

Before a session, make voluntary participation and consent practical, not ceremonial. Explain who is conducting the interview, its purpose, what will happen, whether anyone will observe, whether you will take notes or record, what information will be collected, who may receive it, how long it will be kept, and how a participant can decline or stop. Seek separate, clear permission for a recording instead of assuming that joining the call authorizes it. Government guidance is written for its own setting and legal regime, so it should not be read as universal legal advice. Still, these disclosures express a sound ethical baseline. Applicable privacy, consumer-protection, employment, accessibility, and research rules vary by location, industry, participant, and data type; obtain appropriate local advice when the stakes or data warrant it.

Keep the data footprint small. Do not collect a full name, address, sensitive history, or recording merely because it might be convenient later. Separate contact details from research notes when possible, restrict access, use secure storage appropriate to the setting, and remove identifiers from findings when identity is not necessary. Notes and recordings can contain personal information even when the discussion seems routine. A person must understand the intended use before agreeing to it.

Analysis begins soon after the round. Preserve an observation separately from the interpretation it may suggest. “Participant 04 checked three messaging apps before finding the update” is an observation. “Tutors need a new messaging platform” is an interpretation and a proposed solution; it does not follow automatically. Extract relevant observations from notes or an authorized recording, label the participant context, and sort similar observations into provisional themes. Then write a bounded finding: for example, “Several interviewed tutors described missing schedule changes when updates were spread across more than one channel.” Report contrary cases too. Finally, identify what the evidence supports, what it does not establish, and the next question. That discipline turns interview notes into an auditable learning record rather than a collection of memorable anecdotes.

vocabulary.definition: A planned conversation with a person who has relevant experience, used to learn about their context, actions, language, and constraints.
A short, flexible plan of topics and prompts that keeps interviews comparable without requiring a rigid script.
A question that invites a participant to describe an experience in their own words rather than select a fixed or yes-or-no answer.
A question whose wording suggests a preferred answer or assumes an unverified conclusion.
Selecting participants because their experience or characteristics are relevant to a defined learning question, not because they form a random sample.
A participant's voluntary agreement after receiving understandable information about the activity, data handling, recording, and intended use.
A record of what a participant said or did, kept distinct from the researcher's explanation of its meaning.
A provisional pattern or shared topic formed by organizing related observations across interview notes.

eli10.simplifiedExplanation:
A customer interview is like asking someone to show you how they pack for a trip. Instead of saying, “Would you like my amazing suitcase?” you ask, “Tell me about the last trip you packed for. What did you bring? What was hard?” Their story can show what they actually do and what gets in the way. You listen, ask a few gentle follow-up questions, and write down what happened.

You must also be fair. Tell the person why you are asking, whether you are recording, and what will happen to their information. They can say no or stop. Do not collect private details you do not need. After several conversations, look for patterns, but do not pretend that a few people speak for every traveler in the world.
eli10.analogy: Think of the interviews as several flashlight beams in a dark room. Each beam helps you see one part of the room and may reveal a pattern, but a few beams do not measure the whole building. You still need to say where you looked and where you did not.
eli10.analogyLimits: People are not objects to inspect, and an interview is a conversation that needs consent and respect. Also, a pattern in notes is not automatically a business decision or proof that a proposed solution is wanted.

workedExample: Mina is considering a service that helps independent tutors track schedule changes. Her interview goal is not “prove tutors want my service.” It is “understand what tutors do when a recurring session changes and what makes the process difficult.” She recruits five tutors who currently schedule recurring sessions, noting that three use text messages, two use calendar links, and one works with an assistant. Before each call, Mina explains that participation is voluntary, she will take notes but not record unless the person separately agrees, and she will remove names from her summary. She asks, “Walk me through the last time a family changed a session.” When one tutor says, “I usually lose the update,” Mina asks, “What happened after you noticed?” rather than “Would reminders solve that?” Her notes show that three tutors described updates spread across channels; two did not experience that issue because they use a shared calendar. Mina reports a pattern among these interviewees, the counterexamples, and a next question about the conditions that make a shared calendar workable. She does not claim that five interviews establish how common the burden is or that her service is validated.

commonMistakes.mistake: Recruiting only friends, fans, or the easiest contacts and treating them as the market.
commonMistakes.correction: Set criteria tied to the learning question, seek relevant variation, and disclose the sample's likely bias and limits.

commonMistakes.mistake: Asking participants to approve a solution or predict a future purchase.
commonMistakes.correction: Ask for a concrete past episode, actions taken, alternatives used, and conditions that shaped the outcome.

commonMistakes.mistake: Turning silence or a vague answer into an opportunity to explain the preferred answer.
commonMistakes.correction: Pause, ask a neutral follow-up, or move on; the interviewer's job is to learn, not persuade.

commonMistakes.mistake: Recording or retaining personal information without clear disclosure and permission.
commonMistakes.correction: Explain data and recording plans, collect only what is needed, protect access, and follow applicable local requirements.

commonMistakes.mistake: Writing a solution claim as though it were an observation.
commonMistakes.correction: Keep notes on what was said or done separate from interpretations, themes, and proposed next steps.

compareContrast.distinction: An interview seeks contextual depth and exploratory patterns; a representative survey is designed to estimate responses in a defined population. A small interview sample cannot substitute for the latter.
An open, neutral question invites the participant's account; a leading question embeds the interviewer's preferred answer or an unsupported assumption.
An observation records what happened or was said; an interpretation proposes what it may mean and must remain open to revision.

keyTakeaway: Customer interviews are an ethical, exploratory way to learn from relevant people's real experiences. Plan around a focused question, listen without steering, protect participants and their data, and report themes as bounded evidence—not proof of a market or solution.

questionBank.prompt: Which statement best describes the evidence limit of a small, purposively recruited customer-interview round?
options: It can reveal contextual patterns and sharpen questions, but it does not estimate how common a view is across a market.
It proves the percentage of all potential customers who will buy a product.
It eliminates the need to state who was interviewed.
It makes statistical sampling unnecessary for any later question.
questionBank.explanation: Small interview rounds can produce useful qualitative insights, but they do not provide a population estimate. The other options incorrectly turn exploratory evidence into representative measurement or remove the need for transparent sampling limits.
questionBank.skill: Recall the appropriate scope of interview evidence.

questionBank.prompt: A founder wants to learn about last-minute schedule changes. Which opening question is most neutral and likely to elicit a concrete experience?
options: Don't you think schedule-change apps are frustrating to use?
Tell me about the last time a schedule changed. What happened?
Would you pay for an app that fixes schedule chaos?
How frustrating and expensive was the confusing process?
questionBank.explanation: B asks for a real episode without assuming a problem, cause, or solution. A and D lead the participant; C asks for a hypothetical purchase response rather than an account of current behavior.
questionBank.skill: Choose an open, neutral prompt for a customer interview.

questionBank.prompt: During a session, a participant says, “I missed the update because I was teaching.” What is the best immediate follow-up?
options: So automatic reminders would solve it, right?
Why did you ignore the update?
Can you tell me more about what happened after you were teaching?
You should switch to our calendar system.
questionBank.explanation: C invites detail about the participant's experience without supplying an explanation or a solution. A and D steer toward a product; B is accusatory and assumes fault.
questionBank.skill: Use a non-leading follow-up to understand a participant's account.

questionBank.prompt: Which practice best respects informed participation and privacy when an entrepreneur plans to record interviews?
options: Start recording before the participant joins so the introduction is captured.
Record everyone by default because an invitation implies consent.
Collect every available personal detail in case it becomes useful later.
Explain the purpose, recording, data use, sharing, and retention in understandable terms; obtain voluntary permission and collect only what is needed.
questionBank.explanation: D combines clear, voluntary consent with data minimization. The other practices assume permission, conceal recording, or collect unnecessary personal information.
questionBank.skill: Identify ethical consent and privacy practices for interview research.

questionBank.prompt: After five interviews, three tutors describe checking multiple channels before finding schedule updates, while two rely on a shared calendar and do not report that issue. Which finding is best supported?
options: Several interviewed tutors described a multi-channel update burden, while the pattern did not appear in every interview; investigate the conditions behind the difference.
All tutors need a new messaging platform.
A majority of the entire tutor market has the same problem.
The team has proven its proposed service will be purchased.
questionBank.explanation: A reports the observed pattern, includes the counterexamples, and sets a bounded next question. B, C, and D overgeneralize from a small qualitative sample and leap to a solution or market-wide conclusion.
questionBank.skill: Write a bounded finding from interview notes without overclaiming.
