questionBank.prompt: Why can a five-year effort still be a project?
options: Any effort lasting over one year is automatically a project.
Projects are defined by their budget, not their ending point.
Long work is always a program instead of a project.
Project temporary means the effort has a beginning and end, not that it is brief.
questionBank.explanation: Temporary refers to the bounded nature of the effort, not its duration. A long effort can remain a project when it is directed to a defined result and ends.
questionBank.skill: Interpret temporary as a bounded effort rather than a short duration.

questionBank.prompt: A dean reviews unrelated work: a building repair, a cybersecurity upgrade, a student-services program, and routine facilities maintenance. The dean prioritizes the overall mix against institutional objectives. What is the best label for that level of management?
options: Operations management, because every item must be recurring.
A program, because all items must deliver one shared outcome.
A project, because the dean is overseeing work with constraints.
Portfolio management, because a broader mix of projects, programs, and related work is being managed.
questionBank.explanation: Portfolio management considers a broader collection of projects, programs, and related work in relation to organizational objectives. The items need not be one related program.
questionBank.skill: Distinguish a portfolio from a project or program.

quickCheck.prompt: Which feature is essential to identifying work as a project?
options: It is performed by more than one person.
It uses a written schedule.
It is a temporary effort to create a defined result.
It happens within a business or school.
quickCheck.explanation: A project is temporary and directed toward a defined product, service, result, or change. Teams, schedules, and organizational settings can occur in both projects and operations.
quickCheck.skill: Identify the defining features of a project.

quickCheck.prompt: Which situation is most clearly ongoing operations rather than a project?
options: Selecting and launching a new library catalog.
Renovating a science laboratory by a stated date.
Developing instructions for a new student check-in process.
Staffing an established help desk each weekday.
quickCheck.explanation: Staffing an established help desk is recurring service delivery. The other choices describe bounded efforts to create or change something specific.
quickCheck.skill: Distinguish ongoing operations from a project.

quickCheck.prompt: A university coordinates three related projects—new advising software, training for advisors, and redesigned appointment procedures—to improve student access. What best describes the coordinated effort?
options: An operational shift because each activity is recurring.
A portfolio because the work cannot have a shared outcome.
A program because related projects are being coordinated for a broader outcome.
A single project because all the work involves students.
quickCheck.explanation: A program coordinates related projects and work to achieve broader outcomes or benefits. The scenario gives the projects a shared student-access outcome.
quickCheck.skill: Classify coordinated related projects as a program.

title: Project Life Cycle
in30Seconds: A project life cycle is a way to organize a temporary project from its beginning to its end. It divides the work into meaningful phases, each with related activities and a result to review or hand off. The labels, number, order, and amount of overlap are not universal. A useful life cycle makes the next decision, expected evidence, and transition clear while fitting the kind of work being done.
whyItMatters: A life cycle gives a team a shared way to see where work stands without pretending every project follows the same recipe. It helps students distinguish a phase from a task, identify what evidence should support a transition, and notice when a project needs to revisit earlier work. Those habits support later lessons on scope, schedules, risk, quality, and change control. A life cycle is an organizing and learning tool; it cannot guarantee a project’s schedule, cost, quality, or outcome.
learningObjectives: Define a project life cycle as a project-specific arrangement of phases from beginning to end.
Distinguish a phase, a deliverable, a decision gate, and a project-management process group.
Explain why phase names and relationships should be adapted to the work rather than treated as universal.
Apply an evidence-based transition check to a simple project scenario.
Analyze when iteration or overlap is more informative than a strictly linear picture.

collegeVersion.heading: A life cycle is a structure for the whole temporary effort
collegeVersion.body:
A project has a beginning and an end, but neither fact tells a team how to organize the work in between. A project life cycle supplies that organizing structure. It groups related activities into phases so people can make sense of progress, coordinate handoffs, and decide when the project is ready to move forward. The Project Management Institute describes phases as collections of logically related activities that culminate in one or more deliverables. In this sense, a phase is larger than an individual task. Drafting a test plan may be a task; completing the work needed to produce, inspect, and approve an agreed test-ready version can be part of a phase.

A life cycle should not be confused with the useful life of a product, service, or facility. A project may create a service that continues for years after the project closes. The project life cycle concerns the temporary effort that produces, changes, or transitions that result. It also should not be confused with process groups. A process group names a kind of management activity, such as planning or monitoring, that may recur in several phases. A phase instead locates related work in the project’s overall progression. One phase can involve planning, executing, monitoring, and communicating at the same time. Keeping these ideas separate prevents an attractive four-word diagram from becoming a false description of every team’s actual work.

A general educational model can use four broad questions: What needs to be understood before substantial commitment? What must be organized or designed? What must be created, tested, or delivered? How will the result be transitioned and the temporary effort closed? These questions can be useful as an orientation, but they are not a mandatory framework. PMI lists common phase names such as feasibility, design, build, and test. Construction, research, event, software, and community projects can use different names, deliverables, relationships, and controls. The purpose is intelligible coordination, not conformity to a single vocabulary.

collegeVersion.heading: Phases make transitions and evidence visible
collegeVersion.body:
A phase has a purpose, related activities, and an output or condition that allows people to assess what comes next. That output might be a reviewed prototype, a tested service process, an approved design, a trained group of users, or a documented handoff. It is not enough merely to announce that a calendar date has arrived. A responsible transition asks whether the relevant evidence exists and whether it supports the next commitment. The decision can be to proceed, revise, pause, change the order of work, or stop. This is why a phase boundary can be useful even when work is not strictly sequential.

A decision gate, sometimes called a stage gate, is a deliberately defined point for that decision. The gate is not a ceremonial meeting and it is not a guarantee that the next phase will be trouble-free. It connects a decision to stated exit criteria and evidence. In GAO’s technology-readiness guide, a phased acquisition example moves from one broad phase to another through a documented, evidence-based review of knowledge gained, progress, goals, and exit criteria. The guide also explains that an organization can divide a phase into narrower decision points and must make a model that fits its own processes. That is a valuable general lesson, while the guide’s technology-specific assessments and thresholds are not a universal template for ordinary projects.

A team can make a gate more concrete by writing three items: the decision to be made, the evidence needed, and the people responsible for reviewing it. For a hypothetical campus orientation website, a gate before broad release might ask whether the content is accurate, whether a small group can complete the main tasks, and whether the support team knows how to handle questions. A passed gate does not mean the site is perfect. It means the stated evidence is sufficient for the stated next step. If testing reveals that users cannot find accessibility information, the honest choice may be to revise the design and test again rather than declare the project late and move on anyway. This example describes an analytical practice, not advice about an organization’s approval rules.

collegeVersion.heading: Adapt the pattern to uncertainty, feedback, and constraints
collegeVersion.body:
Some work benefits from a relatively predictive sequence: a team may need an approved design before it can safely construct a physical component. Other work benefits from shorter cycles of building, observing, and revising because important details become clear only when users or experiments provide feedback. Many projects combine both patterns. A project can have an overall sequence of preparation, development, delivery, and transition while teams iterate within a development phase. It can also overlap carefully chosen activities when doing so does not create unacceptable rework or risk. The question is not which label is superior. The question is which arrangement makes dependencies, uncertainty, commitments, and learning visible enough for this project.

Adaptation has limits. Changing phase names does not erase a dependency, and calling a review agile does not make missing evidence acceptable. If a later activity relies on an earlier decision, the life cycle should show the relationship and define how a change will be handled. A team should also avoid treating a phase as a silo in which only one specialty participates. Testing, stakeholder communication, risk review, and learning can occur throughout a project even when a particular deliverable or decision is concentrated in one phase. The next lessons examine several of those activities separately.

The useful level of detail depends on the project. A two-person student event may need a short list of checkpoints and clear ownership. A high-consequence technical acquisition may require formal evidence reviews and several stages inside a broad phase. More gates are not automatically better; unnecessary gates can slow learning and obscure responsibility. Too few can hide assumptions until commitments are expensive to change. The life cycle should therefore be revisited as the team learns. Revising it is not proof of failure. It can be an appropriate response when the work, its risks, or the evidence needed for a sound decision becomes clearer.

vocabulary.definition: The project-specific arrangement of phases that organizes a temporary effort from its beginning through its end.
A logical grouping of related project activities with a defined purpose and one or more results to review.
A verifiable result, capability, or item produced by project work and made available for review or handoff.
A defined point where responsible people use stated evidence and criteria to decide whether and how work should continue.
Conditions or evidence agreed in advance to assess whether a phase is ready for a transition decision.
A repeated cycle of doing work, obtaining feedback or evidence, and revising the work based on what was learned.
The transfer of a deliverable, information, responsibility, or capability from one role, group, or phase to another.

eli10.simplifiedExplanation:
A project life cycle is like dividing a big class production into understandable parts. Before the show, people need to learn what it is supposed to accomplish. Then they organize and make things, rehearse or test them, and finally hand the result to the audience and clean up the temporary work. The parts help everyone ask, “What are we trying to finish now, and what tells us we are ready for the next part?”

Different projects need different parts. A science experiment may repeat testing many times. A stage set may need its design checked before building begins. The point is not to force every project through the same four boxes. It is to choose a path that helps people learn, make decisions, and avoid acting as if a guess were already proven.
eli10.analogy: Think of a relay race plan. Each runner has a section of the track, and the handoff zone makes the transfer visible. A project phase is like a section of that plan, while a decision gate is a checkpoint asking whether the next runner has what they need to continue safely and usefully.
eli10.analogyLimits: Projects are not relay races with one fixed route and a single runner at a time. Teams often work in parallel, return to earlier questions, or change the route after new evidence. A gate also does not automatically approve work; people must examine relevant evidence and make a judgment.

workedExample: River City Library is hypothetically creating a one-day neighborhood storytelling event. Its team first explores whether there is enough interest, a suitable space, and accessible ways for people to participate. It then develops the program, confirms volunteers, and prepares materials. Before promoting the event widely, the team holds a transition check: the schedule is complete, the room is confirmed, accessibility information is accurate, and a small pilot activity has shown that the sign-up instructions are understandable. If the pilot reveals that people cannot use the form on phones, the team revises and tests it again. On event day, delivery and observation occur together; afterward, the team transfers attendance records and lessons learned to the library’s ongoing staff and closes temporary arrangements. The example uses a tailored life cycle, not a prescribed method or a guarantee of attendance.

commonMistakes.mistake: Treating every project life cycle as the same list of named phases.
commonMistakes.correction: Use common labels as examples, then define phases, relationships, and evidence for the actual kind of work.

commonMistakes.mistake: Assuming a phase ends because its planned date has arrived.
commonMistakes.correction: Use the date as a prompt to review stated exit criteria and evidence, then decide whether to proceed, revise, pause, or stop.

commonMistakes.mistake: Equating a decision gate with automatic approval.
commonMistakes.correction: A gate is a decision point; the evidence can support revision, added learning, a different path, or no continuation.

commonMistakes.mistake: Believing iterative work has no life cycle.
commonMistakes.correction: Iterative work can still have an overall beginning and end, phases, transitions, and repeated feedback loops within them.

compareContrast.distinction: A project life cycle organizes the temporary effort that creates or changes a result; a product or service life cycle concerns the result’s continuing existence or use.
A phase locates related work in the project’s progression; a process group describes a type of management activity that may recur in more than one phase.
A decision gate requires an evidence-based choice about the next step; a milestone marks a significant event or point and may or may not include a formal decision.

keyTakeaway: A project life cycle is a tailored structure for moving a temporary effort from beginning to end. Its value comes from making phases, evidence, transitions, and learning visible—not from copying a fixed set of labels or promising a particular outcome.

questionBank.prompt: Which description best defines a project life cycle?
options: A tailored arrangement of project phases from beginning to end.
The period during which a completed product remains popular.
A list of every task assigned to one person.
A guarantee that a project will meet its budget.
questionBank.explanation: A project life cycle organizes the temporary project through related phases. It is not a product’s market history, one person’s task list, or a guarantee about cost.
questionBank.skill: Recall the purpose and scope of a project life cycle.

questionBank.prompt: What makes a decision gate different from simply reaching a calendar milestone?
options: It requires every task in the entire project to be complete.
It uses stated criteria and evidence to decide how work should continue.
It prevents a team from revisiting earlier work.
It always authorizes the next phase without discussion.
questionBank.explanation: A decision gate links evidence and criteria to a choice about proceeding, revising, pausing, or stopping. A date alone does not establish readiness or force approval.
questionBank.skill: Distinguish an evidence-based transition decision from a calendar event.

questionBank.prompt: A team has finished a prototype, but user testing shows that people cannot complete the main task. Which response best applies life-cycle thinking?
options: Move to launch because the prototype phase has a scheduled end date.
Delete the test results because they slow the project.
Use the evidence to revise the design and test again before making the next commitment.
Declare that iterative work cannot use phases.
questionBank.explanation: The test result is evidence for the transition decision. Revising and retesting can be the appropriate response; a date does not make inadequate evidence sufficient.
questionBank.skill: Apply exit evidence to determine a responsible next step.

questionBank.prompt: Which life-cycle design is most defensible for a project that must refine an unfamiliar service through repeated user feedback while also meeting a fixed public-event date?
options: Use no phases because feedback makes planning impossible.
Choose a single universal framework and prohibit all changes.
Separate all testing from delivery so that feedback cannot affect the work.
Use an overall sequence toward the event while allowing short feedback-and-revision cycles where uncertainty is high.
questionBank.explanation: A hybrid arrangement can preserve a visible overall transition while using iteration to learn where details are uncertain. The other choices either deny dependencies or block learning without justification.
questionBank.skill: Analyze how a life cycle can be adapted to both a fixed transition and uncertainty.

questionBank.prompt: Why might two sound projects use different phase names or numbers of gates?
options: Their work, risks, dependencies, and evidence needs can differ.
Only one of the projects is a real project.
A life cycle must always contain exactly four phases.
Phase names determine whether the final result is valuable.
questionBank.explanation: A useful life cycle is tailored to the project and organization. Different work can require different phase structures and transition evidence; labels alone do not create value.
questionBank.skill: Explain why a life cycle is adapted rather than universal.

title: Project Initiation
in30Seconds: Project initiation is the early work of deciding whether a proposed effort should become a project and, if so, giving it permission to begin. It makes the reason for the effort, the intended high-level result, the responsible sponsor, and the people affected visible enough for an informed start. Initiation is not a detailed work plan or a promise that the project will succeed. It is a decision-and-alignment stage before deeper planning.
whyItMatters: Projects often begin with an appealing idea, an urgent complaint, or a request from one person. Initiation turns that starting point into questions that can be examined: What need or opportunity is being addressed? Who can authorize the effort? Who may use, support, fund, operate, or be affected by its result? Answering those questions early makes assumptions discussable and gives later planning a clearer starting point. It does not replace research, requirements work, or organizational approval procedures.
learningObjectives: Define project initiation as early authorization and alignment work.
Explain why a high-level goal differs from a detailed plan or scope baseline.
Distinguish the general role of a project sponsor from the role of a project manager.
Identify stakeholder categories that should be considered early in a hypothetical project.
Analyze what information is still missing before an initiation decision can be responsible.

collegeVersion.heading: Initiation turns a proposal into an examinable project decision
collegeVersion.body:
A project can start as a possibility: a community group wants a new event, a department sees a recurring problem, or a team has an idea for a service. Project initiation is the early work that makes the possibility clear enough to decide whether to begin a temporary effort. In general terms, it connects a stated need or opportunity with an intended result, a source of authorization, and an initial view of the people connected to the work. It answers a narrow but important question: is there enough shared understanding and authority to move from an idea into further project work?

That question is deliberately narrower than “is every detail known?” An initiation decision can acknowledge uncertainty. It may identify information gaps, ask for more investigation, permit a limited exploratory effort, or decide not to proceed. Treating initiation as a moment of certainty encourages teams to hide unknowns. Treating it as an informed decision under limited information makes unknowns visible and gives later work a purpose. The Project Management Institute describes initiating as defining a new project or phase by obtaining authorization to start it. The wording is useful because authorization distinguishes a project from informal enthusiasm or unapproved activity.

The early goal should be expressed at a level that can guide a decision without pretending to specify every future requirement. For a hypothetical library project, “make it easier for residents to find upcoming programs on a phone” states a need and intended direction. It does not yet decide every feature, interface, schedule, vendor, or measurement method. Those later choices belong to neighboring lessons on project charters, scope, requirements, scheduling, and planning. Keeping that boundary matters: an initiation lesson should help learners recognize a well-framed starting question, not hand them an organization-specific approval package.

collegeVersion.heading: A sponsor provides authorization and a connection to the reason for the work
collegeVersion.body:
A project sponsor is generally the person or group with sufficient standing to support the project’s purpose and authorize the project to begin under the organization’s own rules. The sponsor is not simply a ceremonial name. In PMI’s discussion of sponsorship, the role connects the project to a perceived need and its justification, and the sponsor authorizes the project’s start. The exact title, authority, and process vary. A student project may have a faculty sponsor; a public project may have formal governance; a small volunteer effort may use a different form of agreement. This lesson therefore describes a role, not a universal job title or an instruction about who should approve work.

A useful early sponsor conversation tests whether the proposed project has a credible reason to exist. It can clarify the problem or opportunity, the hoped-for result, the high-level benefit, and the constraints or unanswered questions that deserve attention before greater commitment. The U.S. Government Accountability Office’s IT investment framework offers a bounded public-sector example: it links each IT project to an identified business need or mission goal, identifies an executive sponsor, and records users associated with the need. That is not a template for all projects, but it illustrates why authorization is stronger when it is tied to a reason rather than merely to a request.

The sponsor and project manager are also different roles, even though one person can sometimes hold more than one responsibility in a small effort. At a high level, the sponsor supports the project’s rationale and authorization; the project manager coordinates the temporary work after it begins. Initiation benefits when learners can name that distinction without converting it into a rigid hierarchy. Detailed authority limits, project-charter contents, resource allocation, and governance mechanisms are intentionally outside this lesson.

collegeVersion.heading: Early stakeholder identification is mapping, not forced agreement
collegeVersion.body:
A stakeholder is an individual, group, or organization that can affect a project, be affected by it, use its result, supply knowledge or resources, or have an interest in the outcome. During initiation, identification is high level. The aim is to notice whose perspectives could change the decision or reveal a missing condition. For the library example, this might include residents who use the program listing, library staff who maintain information, accessibility advocates, people who provide technical support, and the sponsor responsible for the project’s purpose. A list is not a claim that all stakeholders have equal power, the same needs, or an obligation to agree.

The GAO framework’s IT example identifies specific end-user or customer groups and treats their participation as relevant through the project life cycle. PMI likewise notes that identifying stakeholders early helps sponsors and project managers understand who must be involved and what support or contributions may be needed. The transferable lesson is not to copy either organization’s process. It is to ask broad discovery questions: Who experiences the current problem? Who will use or operate the result? Who may be affected indirectly? Who holds essential knowledge, approval authority, or resources? What do we not yet know about their concerns?

Identification should not become a complete communication plan, a negotiation strategy, or a promise that every concern can be satisfied. Those are later and context-dependent activities. At initiation, a concise stakeholder map can expose a flaw in an otherwise attractive proposal. If the proposed library service assumes every resident has a smartphone, early identification may reveal people who need another way to access information. That finding does not settle a design choice; it shows that the project’s stated need and intended benefit require further investigation before detailed work proceeds.

vocabulary.definition: Early work that frames a proposed project and obtains an appropriate decision about beginning it.
Permission from the responsible authority for a defined effort to begin under applicable arrangements.
A person or group that supports a project’s rationale and has a role in authorizing its start.
A person, group, or organization that affects, is affected by, or has an interest in project work or results.
A stated operational, mission, or service-related reason that a proposed effort is intended to address.
A broad statement of the intended direction or result that guides early decisions without detailing all work.

eli10.simplifiedExplanation:
Initiation is like deciding whether to organize a school fundraiser before anyone starts printing posters or collecting money. First, people need to know the reason for it, what they hope to accomplish, who is allowed to say yes, and who will be affected. Maybe students want new equipment, a teacher can sponsor the effort, families might attend, and the office needs to know about the event. Those facts do not design the fundraiser. They help people decide whether there is a sensible project to organize and what questions need answers next.

A good start can include “we do not know yet.” If nobody has checked whether families can attend at the proposed time, that is important information. The group might learn more before moving ahead rather than acting as though the plan is complete.
eli10.analogy: Think of a movie’s opening credits: they identify who is involved and establish what kind of story is beginning before the full plot unfolds. Initiation similarly makes the purpose, responsible support, and important people visible before detailed project work.
eli10.analogyLimits: A project is not a movie with a fixed script. Initiation can lead to more research, a smaller trial, a changed approach, or a decision not to proceed. Stakeholders also do more than appear in credits: their knowledge and concerns can reshape what the project should investigate.

workedExample: River City Library is hypothetically considering a project to improve how residents find programs on mobile devices. During initiation, the library’s service director asks what problem is being addressed: residents report missing events because information is difficult to find on phones. The director is identified as the sponsor for considering the effort, while staff identify likely stakeholders: residents, front-desk staff, program coordinators, people who use assistive technology, and the team that supports the website. The group does not write a feature list or choose a software provider. It records an early goal—make program information easier to find—and a key gap: it has not yet learned which difficulties different residents experience. The next appropriate step is to investigate that gap before detailed requirements or plans are created.

commonMistakes.mistake: Treating an exciting idea as automatic permission to begin work.
commonMistakes.correction: Separate proposing an idea from obtaining the appropriate authorization and clarifying why the temporary effort should exist.

commonMistakes.mistake: Writing a detailed plan before stating the problem or intended high-level result.
commonMistakes.correction: Start with the need, intended direction, and unknowns; leave detailed scope, requirements, and scheduling to later work.

commonMistakes.mistake: Listing only the people who requested the project as stakeholders.
commonMistakes.correction: Also consider users, people affected by the result, operators, supporters, and holders of essential knowledge or authority.

commonMistakes.mistake: Assuming stakeholder identification means everyone must agree immediately.
commonMistakes.correction: Early identification maps relevant perspectives; it does not settle every decision or eliminate disagreement.

compareContrast.distinction: Initiation frames the reason, authorization, and early participants; detailed planning develops how approved work may be organized and carried out.
A sponsor supports the project’s rationale and authorization, while a project manager coordinates the temporary work; specific arrangements vary by context.
Identification recognizes relevant people and groups; agreement is a separate, context-dependent outcome that may require later communication and decisions.

keyTakeaway: Project initiation creates a responsible starting point by connecting a proposed effort to a high-level need, appropriate authorization, and an early view of stakeholders. Its purpose is alignment and informed decision-making, not a finished plan or guaranteed outcome.

options: A detailed schedule for every project task.
A promise that the intended result will succeed.
Early work that frames a proposed project and obtains a decision about starting it.
A final report written after temporary work ends.

questionBank.prompt: In a general project-management context, what is the sponsor’s most relevant initiation role?
options: Assign every task and monitor daily work.
Provide support for the rationale and participate in authorizing the project’s start.
Write all detailed requirements alone.
Represent every stakeholder’s opinion without distinction.

questionBank.prompt: A museum proposes a digital exhibit but has not considered visitors who use screen readers. What should early stakeholder identification reveal?

All visitors will have identical needs and priorities.

questionBank.prompt: Why can it be responsible for an initiation decision to identify unanswered questions?

They show that the project already has a complete detailed plan.
They make it possible to decide what investigation or limited next step is needed before greater commitment.
They remove the need for any authorization.

questionBank.skill: Explain the role of uncertainty in an initiation decision.

title: Project Charter
in30Seconds: A project charter is an early, high-level record that authorizes a particular project and states why it exists, what it is meant to accomplish, and who has authority to lead it. It gives a shared starting point before detailed planning. A useful charter can name objectives, key assumptions, constraints, major risks, and approval roles without pretending that every requirement, schedule detail, or future decision is already settled.
whyItMatters: A charter turns an idea into work that people can recognize, discuss, and govern. It helps a team distinguish an authorized purpose from an informal wish, identify the person or group accountable for authorization, and surface assumptions before they quietly become commitments. Reading a charter critically also prepares students to notice what still needs discovery and planning. Its value is clarity and traceability, not a promise that the project will meet every target.
learningObjectives: Define a project charter in terms of authorization, high-level direction, and assigned authority.
Identify common high-level charter elements and distinguish them from detailed planning artifacts.
Explain how assumptions, constraints, and risks serve different purposes in an early project record.
Apply charter reasoning to determine what should be clarified before a hypothetical project proceeds.

collegeVersion.heading: A charter establishes authorization and a shared starting point
collegeVersion.body:
A project charter is an early project document issued by a project initiator or sponsor that formally authorizes the project and gives the project manager authority to apply organizational resources to project activities. That definition has two linked parts. Authorization recognizes that the proposed effort is a project the sponsoring organization has chosen to begin. Authority clarifies that a named project manager may coordinate the work within the authority granted. It does not mean that one person can ignore policies, spend without limits, or make every organizational decision alone. The authority is bounded by the organization, the charter, and later governance decisions.

The charter is useful because projects begin with incomplete information. A team may know the reason for a change and the intended result while still needing to learn details about requirements, technical options, timing, risks, or resources. The charter records enough high-level direction to make that early commitment visible. In the PMI lexicon, the initiator or sponsor issues the charter; in practice, the exact approval process and document format can vary by organization. For a college-level analysis, the important question is not whether a file has a particular template. It is whether the record clearly communicates that the project has been authorized, why it matters, who may lead it, and what broad boundaries apply.

A charter is neither a legal contract nor a substitute for an organization’s rules. It is also not a guarantee of funding, success, a completed schedule, or stakeholder agreement. It provides an accountable beginning from which a team can develop and test more detailed plans. The adjacent project-initiation topic considers how an effort is explored and framed before this authorization; the project-scope topic considers the detailed boundary of included and excluded work after the project’s broad direction is established.

collegeVersion.heading: High-level elements make the proposed work intelligible
collegeVersion.body:
Charters differ in length and required fields, but effective high-level records commonly make several questions answerable. What purpose or justification supports the project? What objective or intended result is being pursued? What major requirements, risks, milestones, or resources are already known? Who is sponsoring or authorizing the work, and who is assigned to manage it? GAO’s assessment of project-management documentation lists elements such as purpose or justification, high-level requirements and description, major risks, measurable objectives and success criteria, summary milestones, approval requirements, the assigned manager’s responsibility and authority, and the authorizing sponsor. These are examples of useful categories, not a universal checklist that every project must copy.

The word high-level matters. A charter may say that a hypothetical museum project aims to improve visitor access to its digital collection and that a director sponsors the effort. It need not contain every screen design, every task assignment, or every test result. Those details may emerge through later work. Mixing an early authorization record with a fully detailed plan can create a false impression that uncertainty has already been resolved. Conversely, a one-sentence announcement that names no purpose, authority, or expected result may leave people unable to tell what has actually been authorized.

A useful test is whether a reader can explain the project’s rationale, intended direction, accountable authorization, and major known conditions without mistaking the charter for a complete solution. This is an analytical standard, not advice for a real organization’s approval process. Different kinds of work can reasonably need different levels of formality. A small student event may use a concise record, while a complex public program may require more formal documentation and additional reviews.

collegeVersion.heading: Assumptions, constraints, and risks are not interchangeable
collegeVersion.body:
Early project documents often include assumptions, constraints, and risks because each makes a different kind of uncertainty visible. An assumption is something used for planning or decision-making that has not yet been demonstrated as certain. A hypothetical team might assume that a community room will be available on weekday evenings. A constraint is a limit or condition that restricts choices, such as a fixed event date, an accessibility requirement, or a ceiling on available staff time. A risk is an uncertain event or condition that could affect the project if it occurs; for example, a key supplier might not deliver equipment by the needed date.

The same fact should not be casually placed in all three categories. If a room is confirmed to be unavailable after 6 p.m., that is a constraint, not an assumption. If a team has not yet confirmed availability but is treating it as available while developing an early concept, that is an assumption; the possibility that it will prove unavailable can be recorded as a risk. Separating the categories helps a team see what it should verify, what it must work within, and what could disrupt its intended path. It does not eliminate uncertainty or establish a guarantee that the team will respond perfectly.

A charter should be revised or supplemented through the project’s governance practices when important high-level direction changes. The precise process, authority levels, and timing are organizational decisions, so this lesson does not prescribe them. The educational principle is simpler: material changes should not remain hidden in an outdated starting record. A clear record lets later readers distinguish what was originally authorized from what was learned or decided afterward.

collegeVersion.heading: Read a charter as a decision record, not a ceremonial form
collegeVersion.body:
Consider a hypothetical community college project to create a centralized online orientation hub. A concise charter might state the purpose: reduce the difficulty new students have locating reliable orientation information. It might name a sponsor, assign a project lead, identify a high-level objective such as an accessible, reviewed hub before the next orientation cycle, and record known conditions: the project must use the existing web platform, assumes subject experts can review content during the term, and faces the risk that accessibility testing may reveal redesign work. Those statements make a reasoned early commitment visible.

The same charter should not claim that every page has been approved, that student use will automatically improve, or that the final schedule has been proven. A reader should ask what evidence supports the initial purpose and objectives, whether authority and approval roles are clear, and which assumptions need verification. Questions about detailed inclusion and exclusion belong in scope work; questions about decomposing tasks and estimating timing belong in later planning work. Keeping those boundaries clear makes the charter more honest and more useful.

Good charter reasoning therefore balances commitment and humility. It commits enough information to authorize and orient a project, while labeling important unknowns rather than hiding them. The artifact is valuable when it helps people make subsequent decisions with shared context—not when it is treated as a ceremonial document that makes uncertainty disappear.

vocabulary.definition: An early document that formally authorizes a project and grants the project manager authority to apply organizational resources to project activities.
A person or group with authority to champion, authorize, or provide direction for a project within an organization’s governance structure.
A recognized decision that permits a project or activity to proceed within stated limits.
A stated result or condition the project intends to achieve, used to give its work direction.
A planning condition treated as true or available for the moment, even though it has not been confirmed as certain.
A limit or condition that restricts the choices available to a project.
An uncertain event or condition that could affect a project if it occurs.
Stated measures or conditions used to judge whether a project’s intended result has been achieved.

eli10.simplifiedExplanation:
A project charter is like a short, shared note that says, “Yes, we are going to try this project, here is why, and this is who can organize the first steps.” It is useful before people rush into work because it gives everyone the same starting picture.

The note does not contain every tiny decision. If a class is planning a science fair, it might say the fair should help students share investigations, name the teacher who can coordinate it, and list a fixed date. It could also say that the gym is assumed to be available and that bad weather might affect deliveries. Those are clues about what the team knows and what it still needs to check.
eli10.analogy: Think of a charter as a trailhead sign before a group hike. The sign names the trail, explains the destination, identifies the group leader, and warns about a known closure or weather concern. It helps the group begin with the same orientation.
eli10.analogyLimits: A project is not a hike with one fixed path. Projects can change as people learn, and a trailhead sign does not represent formal sponsorship, resource authority, or organizational governance. The analogy also cannot decide what a real organization must approve.

workedExample: The River City Library is hypothetically considering an online program that lets residents reserve time with a digital-skills volunteer. Its charter states a purpose—make initial help easier to find—and assigns a library manager as sponsor and a staff lead to coordinate early work. It identifies a high-level objective: offer a reviewed pilot before the fall term. It records an assumption that volunteers can cover two evenings per week, a constraint that the pilot must use the library’s existing scheduling system, and a risk that privacy review could require changes. The charter does not select every volunteer, promise participation, or specify each screen in the system. Those details require later planning and evidence. The example illustrates a way to read an early decision record; it is not operational advice for a library.

commonMistakes.mistake: Treating a charter as a legally binding contract.
commonMistakes.correction: Treat it as a project authorization and direction record; legal effect, if any, depends on the actual document and organization, not the label alone.

commonMistakes.mistake: Assuming the charter must contain a complete project plan.
commonMistakes.correction: Keep its direction high-level and use later planning artifacts for detailed scope, tasks, estimates, and controls.

commonMistakes.mistake: Calling every unknown a risk.
commonMistakes.correction: Separate a planning assumption, a binding constraint, and an uncertain event or condition that could affect the project.

commonMistakes.mistake: Treating authorization as unlimited personal authority for the project manager.
commonMistakes.correction: Authority is granted within stated and organizational limits; it does not remove governance, policy, or approval responsibilities.

compareContrast.distinction: A charter authorizes and orients a project at a high level; a detailed plan explains how work is intended to be carried out and controlled.
An assumption is provisionally treated as true for planning; a constraint is a condition that limits choices.
A sponsor or initiator authorizes and supports the project within governance; a project manager coordinates project activities within granted authority.

keyTakeaway: A project charter makes an early project commitment visible: it records the purpose and high-level direction, identifies authorization and granted authority, and surfaces major conditions that still need verification. It guides further work without pretending to be a legal contract or a complete plan.

questionBank.prompt: Which statement best describes the core role of a project charter?
options: It lists every task and estimate needed to complete the project.
It replaces an organization’s policies and approval processes.
It formally authorizes a project and gives the project manager authority to apply organizational resources to project activities.
It guarantees that stakeholders will agree with the final result.
questionBank.explanation: A charter recognizes and authorizes the project and grants defined project authority. It is not a complete plan, a replacement for governance, or a guarantee of agreement.
questionBank.skill: Recall the authorization purpose of a project charter.

questionBank.prompt: Which item is most appropriate as high-level charter information rather than a detailed planning artifact?
options: A minute-by-minute assignment for each person during every project week.
The full wording of every test case for a future system.
A complete work breakdown structure with all individual work packages.
A stated purpose, major objective, known high-level risk, and the person authorizing the project.
questionBank.explanation: A charter commonly records purpose, objectives, major known conditions, and authorization at a high level. Detailed assignments, test cases, and work decomposition belong to later planning work.
questionBank.skill: Distinguish high-level charter direction from detailed planning artifacts.

questionBank.prompt: A team is planning around the belief that a campus room will be available, but the reservation has not been confirmed. How should it classify that statement in its early project record?
options: As a success criterion, because the room will make the project successful.
As a constraint, because the team has already been prohibited from using the room.
As an assumption, because the team is provisionally treating an unconfirmed condition as true for planning.
As proof that the schedule is complete.
questionBank.explanation: The unconfirmed availability is an assumption used for planning. A confirmed limit would be a constraint; neither a success criterion nor a complete schedule follows from the statement.
questionBank.skill: Apply the distinction between an assumption and a constraint.

questionBank.prompt: A charter names a sponsor, a project manager, a high-level objective, and a major accessibility risk. What is the strongest conclusion?
options: The project manager may disregard accessibility requirements because the charter mentions a risk.
The project has already resolved every requirement and design decision.
The sponsor no longer has any governance role once the project manager is named.
The charter provides an accountable high-level starting point, while detailed decisions and risk responses still require later work.
questionBank.explanation: The charter records early direction and responsibility, not a completed solution. Naming a risk makes uncertainty visible; it does not remove requirements, sponsorship, or the need for planning.
questionBank.skill: Analyze the limits of a charter in a project scenario.

questionBank.prompt: Why is it useful to record major assumptions and risks in a project charter?
options: It makes all future events predictable.
It avoids the need to verify uncertain conditions later.
It reveals important conditions the team is relying on or may need to address as later decisions are made.
It converts the charter into a legal contract.
questionBank.explanation: Recording major assumptions and risks helps people see the conditions that support or could affect the early commitment. It does not predict the future, eliminate verification, or create legal status by itself.
questionBank.skill: Explain how early records make uncertainty visible.

title: Project Scope
in30Seconds: Project scope describes the work and deliverables a project is meant to include, along with useful boundaries on what it will not include. A clear scope connects a project’s purpose to observable outputs and acceptance criteria—the conditions used to judge whether an output is ready to accept. Scope can change when circumstances warrant it, but an unreviewed expansion of work can create confusion and strain resources.
whyItMatters: Scope gives people a shared way to ask, “What result are we trying to deliver, what work belongs to that result, and how will we recognize it?” That clarity supports discussion, planning, and later evaluation without promising a perfect prediction. It also makes exclusions visible, so an appealing request can be considered instead of silently becoming extra work. Learning the distinction between a justified, reviewed change and uncontrolled scope growth helps students read project cases carefully.
learningObjectives: Define project scope as included work and deliverables, stated with meaningful boundaries.
Distinguish a deliverable, an exclusion, and an acceptance criterion.
Explain why scope is more specific than a project’s broad purpose or charter.
Apply scope boundaries and acceptance criteria to a short hypothetical project.
Analyze why an unreviewed addition differs from a considered scope change.

collegeVersion.heading: Scope makes a project’s intended work and results discussable
collegeVersion.body:
Project scope is the bounded description of what a project is intended to produce and the work needed to produce it. It is not merely a slogan such as “improve service,” and it is not every activity that someone might find useful. A broad purpose can explain why an effort exists; scope translates that direction into a more usable account of included results and work. In practice, the detail appropriate to a scope description depends on the setting and the project’s maturity. Early language can be high level, then become clearer as relevant information is gathered. The educational point is not that one document format fits every project. It is that people need a shared, sufficiently specific basis for deciding whether proposed work belongs to the effort.

A scope description commonly identifies deliverables. A deliverable is a unique, verifiable product, result, or capability a project is expected to produce. A revised public-information page, a tested orientation module, and a handoff guide might all be deliverables in a hypothetical project. A deliverable should not be confused with a hoped-for long-term benefit. A team may deliver an orientation module; whether every new participant feels prepared depends on many conditions after delivery. Keeping output and hoped-for outcome distinct makes project claims more honest.

Scope also benefits from explicit boundaries. An exclusion says that a particular result or activity is outside this project. Exclusions do not declare an idea worthless. They clarify that the idea is not part of the current commitment, unless it is later considered through the project’s own decision process. A boundary can prevent two common errors: assuming that every related need is automatically included, and treating an excluded need as though no one is allowed to discuss it. Scope is a tool for shared decisions, not a way to silence legitimate concerns.

collegeVersion.heading: Deliverables need acceptance criteria, not just attractive descriptions
collegeVersion.body:
A deliverable names what the project is expected to provide. Acceptance criteria name the conditions that must be met before that deliverable can be accepted. The distinction matters because names alone leave room for incompatible interpretations. “Create an accessible event-registration page” says more than “improve registration,” but it still requires a way to determine whether the page meets the agreed conditions. Criteria might specify observable conditions such as whether the required information is present, whether stated accessibility checks have been completed, or whether a designated reviewer has confirmed a defined result. The right criteria depend on the project; this lesson does not prescribe a universal checklist.

Acceptance criteria are not the same as a task list. “Hold a review meeting” describes an activity. “The page contains the required registration fields and passes the agreed review” describes conditions for accepting an output. Nor are acceptance criteria a guarantee that a project will achieve every hoped-for impact. They provide a transparent basis for deciding whether a particular deliverable meets the conditions that were agreed for it. GAO’s project-management discussion describes scope validation as formal acceptance of completed deliverables by comparing actual results with the requirements baseline. That principle illustrates why a vague finish condition causes problems: people may complete work but still disagree about whether it satisfies the intended result.

Criteria should be understandable to the people who must use them. “High quality” may express an aspiration, but by itself it is too ambiguous to resolve a disagreement. A stronger statement ties the deliverable to a concrete, observable condition. Precision does not require pretend certainty. A team can identify what it knows, state which conditions will be used for acceptance, and revise its shared understanding when evidence justifies doing so. The later Requirements lesson addresses how needs and detailed conditions are elicited and represented; the later Quality Management lesson addresses broader quality practices. This lesson stays focused on the role of scope boundaries and acceptance conditions.

collegeVersion.heading: Change can be responsible; uncontrolled expansion is a different problem
collegeVersion.body:
Projects learn. A new accessibility need, a changed regulation, a discovery during testing, or a clearer understanding of a user’s situation may make an original scope incomplete or no longer appropriate. Therefore, change itself is not evidence of poor management. A proposed change can be described, considered against the current scope and constraints, and decided through the governance appropriate to that setting. The precise authority, records, and approval steps vary by organization and project; this general lesson does not provide organizational or contractual advice.

Scope creep is commonly used for an uncontrolled or unreviewed expansion beyond the agreed work. It often arrives in small pieces: “while you are already changing that page, add another form,” followed by “add one more audience,” followed by a request for a new reporting feature. Any individual request may be reasonable. The problem is not that a request exists; the problem is treating added work as free, automatic, or invisible. PMI materials describe explicit exclusions and documented scope as ways to manage expectations, and GAO describes monitoring and managing changes to baseline requirements. Those sources support a practical distinction: a reviewed change updates the shared understanding; a hidden accumulation weakens it.

A scope boundary also has limits. It cannot predict every discovery, guarantee a schedule or budget, settle conflicting stakeholder values, or make a project beneficial. It can, however, make the current commitment visible enough for people to identify variance and make deliberate choices. That is especially valuable in classroom cases: rather than calling every new request “bad,” ask whether it fits the stated deliverables and exclusions, whether it changes acceptance conditions, and whether its consequences have been considered. Detailed requirements, work decomposition, and formal change-control design belong to later lessons.

vocabulary.definition: The bounded description of the work and deliverables a project is intended to include.
A unique, verifiable product, result, or capability produced by a project or part of it.
A stated limit that helps distinguish included work or results from those not included.
A result, activity, or need explicitly identified as outside the current project scope.
Conditions that a deliverable must meet before it is accepted.
An approved reference point for requirements used to compare actual results and changes.
A difference between the current project work or result and its established scope reference.
Uncontrolled or unreviewed expansion of project work or product scope beyond the agreed scope.

eli10.simplifiedExplanation:
Project scope is like making a clear list for a school fair. The list says what the fair team is going to provide, such as three game booths, signs, and a cleanup plan. It also says what the team is not going to provide, such as running a full concert. That does not mean a concert is a bad idea. It means the fair team cannot quietly add it and still pretend the original job is unchanged.

For each item on the list, the team also needs a way to tell when it is finished. “Make signs” is a job. “Each booth has a readable sign with its name, time, and price” is closer to an acceptance criterion. It gives people something they can check together.
eli10.analogy: Think of scope as the border on a puzzle tray. The border does not show every piece of the picture, but it tells you which pieces belong in this puzzle. Deliverables are the completed sections, and acceptance criteria are the checks that tell you whether a section is really complete enough to place in the tray.
eli10.analogyLimits: Real projects are not puzzles with fixed pieces. New information can justify changing their boundaries, and people may disagree about what counts as useful or complete. The analogy also cannot decide who should approve a real change or what an organization’s rules require.

workedExample: A city library has a hypothetical project to create a pilot webpage that helps residents find digital-literacy workshops. Its scope includes one webpage, a workshop calendar drawn from current library information, and a short handoff note for staff. It excludes building a new registration system and creating workshops for every city agency. Acceptance criteria for the webpage include that it lists the agreed workshop details, uses the existing library platform, and is reviewed against the project’s agreed accessibility check. During review, someone asks to add online payment for unrelated events. The request may be worthwhile, but it does not automatically fit the pilot’s scope. The team can record and consider it rather than quietly treating it as included work. This is an illustrative example, not operational advice for a library.

commonMistakes.mistake: Treating a project’s broad purpose as a complete scope description.
commonMistakes.correction: Connect the purpose to included deliverables, work boundaries, and exclusions that people can discuss.

commonMistakes.mistake: Assuming an exclusion means a related idea has no value.
commonMistakes.correction: An exclusion identifies what is not in the current commitment; the idea can still be considered separately or later.

commonMistakes.mistake: Calling a task an acceptance criterion.
commonMistakes.correction: A task is work performed; an acceptance criterion is a condition used to judge whether a deliverable can be accepted.

commonMistakes.mistake: Treating every scope change as scope creep.
commonMistakes.correction: Change can be considered and approved; scope creep refers to expansion that is uncontrolled or unreviewed.

commonMistakes.mistake: Assuming a scope statement guarantees benefits, cost, or schedule outcomes.
commonMistakes.correction: Scope supports clarity and decisions, but it cannot remove uncertainty or guarantee results.

compareContrast.distinction: Purpose explains the high-level reason for an effort; scope bounds the work and deliverables intended to address it.
A deliverable is an output to be produced; acceptance criteria are conditions used to determine whether that output is acceptable.
A reviewed change is deliberately considered and reflected in the shared baseline; scope creep is uncontrolled or unreviewed expansion.

keyTakeaway: Project scope makes the current project commitment visible: what it includes, what it excludes, which deliverables it expects, and how acceptance can be judged. It supports thoughtful change without treating change or success as automatic.

questionBank.prompt: What is the best definition of an acceptance criterion?
options: A task assigned to a team member.
A general hope that the project will help people.
A condition that a deliverable must meet before it is accepted.
Any request received after a project begins.
questionBank.explanation: Acceptance criteria are conditions for accepting a deliverable. A task is an activity, a hoped-for benefit is broader than a deliverable condition, and a request is not automatically a criterion.
questionBank.skill: Recall the role of acceptance criteria.

questionBank.prompt: Which statement is an exclusion in a project scope?
options: The project will not create a new payment system.
The project will produce a pilot information page.
The project team will review the page before handoff.
The project seeks to make information easier to find.
questionBank.explanation: An exclusion identifies work or a result outside the current project. The other options respectively describe an included deliverable, an activity, and a high-level purpose.
questionBank.skill: Distinguish an exclusion from included work and purpose.

questionBank.prompt: A project is producing a workshop webpage. Midway through, a colleague asks the team to add a new citywide event-payment system. What is the strongest first conclusion?
options: The request is automatically included because both items involve events.
The team should reject the idea permanently because it is out of scope today.
The request proves that the original webpage cannot be delivered.
The request is outside the stated scope unless it is considered and incorporated through an appropriate change decision.
questionBank.explanation: A related request is not automatically included. It can be recorded and considered; an exclusion does not make it worthless, and it does not by itself prevent the current deliverable.
questionBank.skill: Apply a scope boundary to a new request.

questionBank.prompt: Which option best distinguishes a deliverable from an acceptance criterion?
options: A deliverable is a project output; an acceptance criterion is a condition used to judge whether that output is acceptable.
A deliverable is an excluded request; an acceptance criterion is an included request.
A deliverable is a long-term benefit; an acceptance criterion is the project charter.
A deliverable is a scope change; an acceptance criterion is a task list.
questionBank.explanation: A deliverable is a verifiable output, while acceptance criteria provide the conditions for accepting it. The other pairs confuse outputs with exclusions, benefits, charters, changes, or task lists.
questionBank.skill: Compare project-scope vocabulary.

questionBank.prompt: Why is an unreviewed stream of small additions a scope concern even if each addition seems useful?
options: It makes every future change prohibited.
It can expand work beyond the shared scope without considering its effects or updating the shared reference.
It guarantees the project will fail its acceptance review.
It means the project has no deliverables.
questionBank.explanation: Unreviewed additions can create uncontrolled scope expansion and confuse the shared commitment. They do not make all change forbidden, guarantee failure, or erase deliverables.
questionBank.skill: Analyze why controlled change differs from scope creep.

title: Requirements
in30Seconds: Requirements turn stakeholder needs, constraints, and intended outcomes into statements that can guide a project’s result. Elicitation asks people what problem they experience and what conditions matter; documentation makes those findings reviewable; validation checks whether the statements fit intended use. Requirements are not the same as a project’s scope boundary, a task list, or a chosen design. Acceptance criteria are the observable conditions used to judge whether a requirement has been met.
whyItMatters: A project can deliver exactly what a team built and still miss what people needed if the need was poorly understood or expressed. Clear requirements give stakeholders and builders a shared object to question: Does this represent the intended outcome? Is it inside the project’s boundary? How would someone recognize that it has been met? These questions reduce ambiguity without claiming that every uncertainty disappears. They are useful for analyzing a hypothetical project, whether its work is organized predictively, iteratively, or through a hybrid approach.
learningObjectives: Define requirements as documented statements of needed conditions or capabilities connected to stakeholder needs and project objectives.
Distinguish stakeholder needs, requirements, project scope, and acceptance criteria.
Explain why elicitation seeks needs, expectations, constraints, and relevant interfaces rather than collecting a single person’s preferred solution.
Identify language that makes a candidate requirement more observable and testable without prescribing a design.
Analyze whether a proposed acceptance criterion actually demonstrates that a stated requirement has been met.

collegeVersion.heading: Requirements translate needs into reviewable statements
collegeVersion.body:
A stakeholder may begin with a need rather than a ready-made requirement. A resident says, “I cannot tell whether the library’s meeting rooms are available.” A staff member says, “We need fewer phone calls about reservations.” An accessibility reviewer says, “The information must work with common assistive technology.” These are valuable inputs, but they differ in viewpoint and level of detail. Requirements work elicits such needs, expectations, constraints, and relevant interfaces, then develops statements that describe conditions or capabilities the project result needs to satisfy. The work is not an exercise in copying the loudest request into a document. It asks what outcome is needed, for whom, under which conditions, and with what evidence.

Elicitation means drawing information out rather than assuming it is already complete. Depending on the project, evidence might come from interviews, observation, existing records, a prototype, or another appropriate way of learning about intended use. No one technique is universally required. Different stakeholders can expose different facts: a person who uses a service may describe a difficulty, a person who operates it may identify an operational constraint, and a person affected indirectly may identify an accessibility or interface condition. Those inputs can conflict or remain incomplete. Discovering that disagreement is useful; it is not a failure of the work.

A requirement should be written so people can examine the intended condition rather than infer it from a vague aspiration. “The reservation information should be easy to use” identifies a concern but leaves key terms undefined. “A visitor can view a room’s available time slots for a selected date without creating an account” is more specific about a capability, though it may still need clarification about supported devices or accessibility. The statement identifies what a result must allow; it does not specify a particular database, screen layout, or vendor. That what-versus-how distinction preserves room for design while keeping the intended outcome visible.

collegeVersion.heading: Scope, requirements, and acceptance criteria answer different questions
collegeVersion.body:
These concepts are connected but not interchangeable. Project scope is the boundary of the effort: it describes what work, result, or area is included and excluded at a chosen level. Requirements are the conditions or capabilities that the included result needs to meet. A scope statement for the hypothetical library project might say that the work covers public display of room availability but excludes changing the room-booking policy. Within that boundary, a requirement might state that a visitor can see available times for a selected room and date. Scope helps test whether a candidate requirement belongs in the effort; it does not by itself say every condition the result must satisfy.

Acceptance criteria are the observable conditions used to determine whether a particular requirement has been met. For the availability-display requirement, criteria might state that a reviewer can select a room and date, see the current available time slots, and receive a clear message when none are available. The criterion is not a broader wish such as “users will love the site,” and it is not a schedule promise such as “finish by Friday.” It describes evidence related to the requirement. Different projects may record criteria beside a requirement, in test material, or in another agreed form; this lesson names the logical relationship rather than requiring a format.

The boundary also prevents a common leap from need to design. “Residents need reliable availability information” is a need. “Use a blue calendar widget from a named supplier” is a design choice. A design choice can become relevant later, but it should not be disguised as the need itself. Separating them lets a team examine whether multiple designs could meet the same requirement. It also makes assumptions and constraints easier to locate. For instance, “use the existing calendar data” may be a constraint, while “the data refreshes every five minutes” may be a candidate requirement that needs a reason and validation.

collegeVersion.heading: Documentation and validation make meaning testable, not permanent
collegeVersion.body:
Documentation gives a requirement an identifiable form that stakeholders can review, question, and relate to the project objective. It can include a unique label, the source or rationale, the requirement statement, known assumptions or dependencies, and acceptance criteria. A traceability record can connect a stakeholder need or business objective to a detailed requirement and then to a test or review activity. That connection is useful because a reader can ask why an item exists and what evidence is supposed to show it was met. It is not proof that the requirement is automatically correct, affordable, or complete.

Validation asks a different question from editing for grammar: if this requirement were satisfied, would the resulting product or service work appropriately in its intended-use environment? The question brings the learner back to the people and circumstances elicitation uncovered. A requirement may be precisely worded but still miss a necessary user condition. For example, a display that shows availability only during the library’s open hours may be clear, yet it may fail a need if residents commonly plan visits at night. Reviewing scenarios, demonstrations, prototypes, or test results can provide evidence for validation, but the appropriate method depends on context.

Requirements can change as evidence improves. That fact does not mean that careful documentation is useless. A dated, reviewable statement makes it possible to distinguish what was understood earlier from what was learned later, and traceability helps reveal which criteria or tests may need reconsideration. This is a conceptual lesson, not organizational change-control advice. It does not tell a real organization who may approve a change, which tool to buy, or how to negotiate competing requests. Its narrower claim is that visible links among needs, requirements, and evidence make reasoning about a project result more accountable.

A documented condition or capability that a project result needs to satisfy in support of an objective.
The activity of drawing out and clarifying stakeholder needs, expectations, constraints, and relevant context.
The defined boundary describing what a project effort or result includes and excludes at a chosen level.
Observable conditions used to judge whether a particular requirement has been satisfied by a delivered result.
Checking whether a requirement or result fits its intended use and the need it is meant to address.
The ability to follow a documented connection among a need, requirement, related decision, and supporting test or review evidence.

eli10.simplifiedExplanation:
Imagine the library wants people to find open meeting rooms without calling the front desk. That is the problem people are having, not yet a full requirement. The group talks with visitors, staff, and people who use accessibility tools to learn what matters. Then it writes a clear statement such as, “A visitor can see available times for a chosen room and date.” Now people can ask whether that is really needed and what would show it works.

The project’s scope is like the fence around a playground: it says this project covers showing availability, not changing the rules for who can book rooms. Acceptance criteria are like the referee’s checks: choose a room and date, see the available times, and get a useful message if none are open. Those checks do not choose the colors or computer code; they show whether the stated requirement was met.
eli10.analogy: Requirements are like a recipe request for a school bake sale. “We need snacks that students with nut allergies can safely identify” states the need. A requirement can say that every snack has a visible ingredient label, while acceptance criteria describe what the label must show when someone checks it.
eli10.analogyLimits: A project is not a recipe with one correct ingredient list. Stakeholders can have competing needs, and a real requirement may involve a service, policy boundary, or technical interface rather than an object. The analogy also does not decide who in an organization approves a requirement.

workedExample: River City Library hypothetically plans a public page for meeting-room availability. Elicitation reveals three inputs: visitors want to know open times before traveling, desk staff need the page not to claim that a room is reserved, and an accessibility reviewer needs the information to be readable with assistive technology. The scope boundary is public availability display; changing reservation policy is excluded. The group writes a candidate requirement: “A visitor can select a room and date and view the current available time slots.” It pairs that with acceptance criteria: a reviewer can make those selections, sees time slots or a clear no-availability message, and can reach the same information using keyboard navigation. The group has not selected a calendar vendor or promised fewer calls. A later review can validate whether the statement and criteria reflect the intended user situation.

commonMistakes.mistake: Treating one stakeholder’s preferred solution as the requirement.
commonMistakes.correction: First identify the underlying need or condition, then distinguish it from a possible design that might meet it.

commonMistakes.mistake: Using scope and requirements as synonyms.
commonMistakes.correction: Use scope for the project boundary and requirements for the conditions or capabilities expected within that boundary.

commonMistakes.mistake: Calling a deadline or an opinion an acceptance criterion.
commonMistakes.correction: Write criteria as observable evidence that a specific requirement has been met.

commonMistakes.mistake: Assuming a well-formatted document proves the requirement fits real use.
commonMistakes.correction: Validate against intended use and stakeholder needs; clear writing and valid content are related but different checks.

compareContrast.distinction: A need expresses a problem, expectation, or desired outcome; a requirement states a condition or capability the result needs to satisfy in response.
Scope sets the included and excluded boundary of the effort; a requirement specifies a needed condition or capability within that boundary.
A requirement states what must be true or possible; acceptance criteria describe the observable conditions used to judge whether it has been met.

keyTakeaway: Requirements make stakeholder needs reviewable by expressing the conditions or capabilities a project result must satisfy. They work with, but are not identical to, scope boundaries and acceptance criteria; validation reconnects the statements to intended use.
