title: Estimating
in30Seconds: A project estimate is a reasoned approximation of an effort, duration, quantity, or cost made from information available at a particular time. It is different from a commitment: an estimate describes a current forecast, while a commitment is a promise or obligation whose meaning depends on context. Estimators may compare similar past work, apply a rate to units, add detailed parts, or draw on relevant expertise. Each approach relies on assumptions and has uncertainty, so an estimate should state its basis and range rather than claim certainty.
whyItMatters: Estimates help people discuss what a proposed project may require before every detail is known. Without them, a project can confuse a rough early forecast with a fixed fact, or make a precise-looking number seem more reliable than its inputs. Learning the main approaches also makes it easier to ask useful questions: What past work is truly comparable? What rate and unit are being used? Which details were included? What assumptions could change the result? These questions improve interpretation of a plan. They do not turn estimation into a guarantee, nor do they decide what any organization should approve, promise, or spend.
learningObjectives: Define an estimate and distinguish it from a commitment.
Compare analogous, parametric, bottom-up, and expert-judgment approaches to estimating.
Explain why assumptions, available information, and uncertainty affect an estimate.
Calculate a simple parametric hypothetical estimate and state the conditions behind it.
Evaluate why a range and a documented basis can be more informative than an unsupported single number.

collegeVersion.heading: An estimate is a current model, not a promise
collegeVersion.body:
An estimate is a reasoned approximation of something a project may require, such as work time, elapsed duration, materials, quantity, or cost. It is built from the information available when the estimate is made. The U.S. Government Accountability Office's estimating guide places purpose, scope, schedule, technical baseline, assumptions, data, methodology, risk, documentation, and updates among the inputs and steps of an estimate. That framing is useful because it treats a number as the visible result of a model, not as a fact detached from its basis. A number with two decimal places can still be highly uncertain if its scope or data are weak.

Estimate and commitment should not be used as synonyms. An estimate says what the analyst currently expects under stated conditions. A commitment can mean a promise, authorization, contract term, target, or other obligation, depending on the setting. This general-education lesson does not advise anyone on obligations or procurement. Its limited point is that calling an estimate a commitment can hide uncertainty and create a false impression that the future is fixed. A careful reader asks whether a statement is a forecast, a target, or an obligation, and what evidence supports it.

Estimates normally change when material information changes. A clearer work description, a revised quantity, new actual results, or a failed assumption can all alter the current approximation. Updating does not prove that an earlier estimate was dishonest or that planning was pointless; it records what is known now. It also does not guarantee a successful schedule or budget outcome. The appropriate use and approval of an estimate are matters for the relevant people and context, outside this lesson.

collegeVersion.heading: Four approaches answer different information problems
collegeVersion.body:
Analogous estimating starts with an earlier, sufficiently similar piece of work and adjusts it for relevant differences. For example, a past community event may offer a rough starting point for a proposed event, but differences in attendance, venue, accessibility needs, or content can make a direct copy misleading. The Project Management for Instructional Designers open textbook describes analogous estimating as scaling a similar prior estimate to the current project. Its speed can be useful early, but similarity and the adjustment must be examined rather than assumed.

Parametric estimating applies a rate or relationship to a measurable quantity. A simple form is units multiplied by a rate per unit. Its usefulness depends on whether the rate, unit, and conditions are relevant to the new situation. It is not enough to multiply correctly: a rate based on different work conditions can produce a precisely calculated but poorly grounded result. In GAO's terminology, parametric methods use relationships between the outcome and one or more parameters; the model's inputs, range, and limitations should be documented.

Bottom-up estimating begins with smaller, defined components and aggregates them. The OER source describes detailed bottom-up work as estimating each detail and adding the pieces. This can make the basis visible, but detail is not automatically accuracy: omitted work, duplicated work, or weak component assumptions still distort the total. Expert judgment uses the informed assessment of people with relevant experience. It can contribute insight where data are sparse, but it should not be treated as an unexplained certainty. A useful estimate can combine approaches as a cross-check, while still naming which evidence and judgment were used.

collegeVersion.heading: Ranges and assumptions make uncertainty visible
collegeVersion.body:
An estimate is conditional. Its assumptions may concern scope, quantities, availability, productivity, technical conditions, calendar, historical data, or the way units are counted. GAO emphasizes documenting ground rules and assumptions, methodology, data limitations, sensitivity, risk, and uncertainty. In introductory terms, that means a reader should be able to ask what must remain true for an estimate to make sense and what would make it change. An unsupported single value can conceal those questions; a range can better communicate that more than one plausible outcome remains. A range is not a guarantee that reality will stay within it.

Consider a hypothetical campus poster project. Suppose the planning model assumes 120 posters, a printing rate of $2.40 per poster, and a separate fixed setup amount of $36. The variable portion is 120 × $2.40 = $288. Adding the setup amount gives $288 + $36 = $324. The arithmetic is checked, but the estimate is conditional: it assumes all 120 posters use the stated rate, the setup amount applies once, the scope includes no delivery fee, and no specifications change. If the quantity changes or the rate applies only to a different paper type, the calculation needs revision.

The example does not say what a real project should buy, charge, approve, or commit. It shows a compact basis of estimate: quantity, rate, fixed component, calculation, and assumptions. A range could be developed by testing alternative plausible inputs, but the selection of any range requires context and evidence. Estimation supports a conversation about uncertainty; it does not remove uncertainty or replace judgment.

vocabulary.definition: A reasoned approximation of a project quantity, effort, duration, or cost based on information and assumptions available at a stated time.
A promise, obligation, target, or authorized undertaking whose exact meaning depends on the setting; it is not automatically an estimate.
An approximation derived from similar prior work and adjusted for relevant differences in the current work.
An approximation calculated by applying a documented rate or relationship to a measurable quantity or other parameter.
An approximation formed by estimating smaller defined components and aggregating their values into a total.
An informed assessment from people with relevant knowledge or experience used as an input to an estimate.
A condition treated as true for planning even though later evidence may confirm, change, or disprove it.
A stated span of plausible estimated values that communicates uncertainty more openly than one unsupported point value.

eli10.simplifiedExplanation:
An estimate is a careful guess, not a magic answer. If you are planning a bake sale, you might guess how many cookies to make and how much ingredients may cost. That guess depends on what you know today, such as the number of people you expect and a price at the store. If either fact changes, the guess may change too.

You can estimate by remembering a similar bake sale, by using a rule such as number of cookies times cost per cookie, by adding every small ingredient cost, or by asking someone who has planned many sales. Each way can help, but each can miss something. A commitment is different: it is a promise or obligation. An estimate should say what it assumes and leave room for uncertainty.
eli10.analogy: An estimate is like predicting how many blocks you need for a model bridge. You might copy a similar bridge, multiply the number of sections by blocks per section, count each piece, or ask an experienced builder.
eli10.analogyLimits: A project involves changing scope, people, conditions, and sometimes money or time. Blocks are simple and interchangeable, so the analogy cannot decide a real commitment, prove a number is correct, or guarantee that a project will finish as forecast.

workedExample: A student club hypothetically plans 120 identical event posters. Its preliminary parametric model uses a printing rate of $2.40 per poster plus one setup amount of $36. The variable portion is 120 × $2.40 = $288. The total is $288 + $36 = $324. This is an estimate, not a commitment or purchase instruction. It rests on stated assumptions: 120 is the final quantity, every poster qualifies for the same rate, setup is charged once, and delivery, tax, design work, and changed specifications are outside the illustrated scope. If one of those assumptions changes, the current estimate should be reconsidered. The calculation demonstrates a rate-times-quantity model; it does not claim a real printer will charge that rate or that the total will occur.

commonMistakes.mistake: Treating an estimate as though it automatically creates a promise.
commonMistakes.correction: Identify whether the statement is a current forecast, a target, or an obligation, and retain the estimate's stated assumptions.

commonMistakes.mistake: Using a prior project as an analogy without examining differences.
commonMistakes.correction: State why the prior work is comparable and how scope, scale, conditions, or complexity have been adjusted.

commonMistakes.mistake: Assuming a correct multiplication proves an estimate is reliable.
commonMistakes.correction: Check the applicability of the rate, quantity, inclusions, exclusions, and conditions as well as the arithmetic.

commonMistakes.mistake: Presenting one number with no uncertainty or basis.
commonMistakes.correction: Document the approach, evidence, assumptions, and where appropriate a range or sensitivity to changed inputs.

compareContrast.distinction: An estimate is a conditional current approximation; a commitment is a promise or obligation whose meaning is set by context.
Analogous estimating adjusts a similar prior case; parametric estimating applies a rate or relationship to a measured input.
Bottom-up estimating aggregates defined components; expert judgment contributes relevant experienced assessment and may inform several methods.

keyTakeaway: An estimate is a transparent, conditional approximation rather than a certainty or automatic commitment. The method, data, assumptions, exclusions, and uncertainty matter as much as the displayed number.

questionBank.prompt: How should a forecast of project cost, duration, or effort be interpreted?
options: A contractual promise to deliver a fixed outcome.
A final number that cannot change once recorded.
A reasoned approximation based on available information and assumptions.
A list of every possible risk in a project.
questionBank.explanation: An estimate is a reasoned current approximation. It depends on its information and assumptions, so it is not automatically a contract, a fixed fact, or a complete risk list.
questionBank.skill: Recall the definition and conditional nature of an estimate.

questionBank.prompt: A planner begins with the cost of a similar earlier project and adjusts it because the new project has a larger quantity. Which approach is being used?
options: Bottom-up estimating.
Parametric estimating.
A commitment calculation.
Analogous estimating.
questionBank.explanation: Analogous estimating starts with a sufficiently similar earlier case and adjusts for differences. A parametric estimate instead applies a rate or relationship to a measured input.
questionBank.skill: Distinguish analogous estimating from other approaches.

questionBank.prompt: A hypothetical model has 75 units at $4 per unit and one fixed amount of $50. What total does the model produce before any assumptions change?
questionBank.explanation: The variable portion is 75 × $4 = $300. Adding the one fixed $50 amount gives $350. This arithmetic result remains conditional on the model's stated inputs.
questionBank.skill: Apply a simple parametric calculation and distinguish variable from fixed components.

questionBank.prompt: Why can a single precise-looking estimate still be uncertain?
options: Because estimates may never use data.
Because its scope, data, assumptions, and conditions may be incomplete or change.
Because bottom-up estimates cannot be added together.
Because an estimate is always an organizational commitment.
questionBank.explanation: Precision in formatting does not remove uncertainty in inputs or assumptions. Documenting the basis and limitations helps readers interpret the number appropriately.
questionBank.skill: Analyze why numerical precision differs from confidence in an estimate.

questionBank.prompt: Which practice best makes a project estimate interpretable to another reader?
options: State the method, relevant data, calculation, assumptions, and important exclusions or uncertainty.
Replace every estimate with a promise before discussing it.
Use only expert judgment and omit its basis.
Report a number without explaining which work it includes.
questionBank.explanation: A useful basis of estimate makes its reasoning visible: method, inputs, calculation, scope, assumptions, limitations, and uncertainty. This supports review without guaranteeing an outcome.
questionBank.skill: Identify transparent documentation practices for conditional estimates.

provenance.rightsStatus: original-synthesis
provenance.scopeNote: General education about estimate types, assumptions, ranges, and transparent arithmetic. It does not provide procurement, legal, financial, organizational, or commitment advice.

title: Budgeting
in30Seconds: Project budgeting organizes cost estimates into a stated plan for the work and time period being considered. A cost baseline is a reference version of that plan for comparison with later information; in PMI terminology, it is time-phased and excludes management reserves. Contingency reserve and management reserve are not interchangeable labels: the former is associated with identified uncertainty in a framework's plan, while the latter is kept separately from the cost baseline in PMI terminology. These are planning concepts, not promises, spending instructions, or financial advice.
whyItMatters: An estimate can explain what individual pieces of work may require, but a budget makes the relationship among those pieces, their timing, and stated uncertainty easier to inspect. Without clear labels, a reader might mistake an estimate for an approved reference, hide uncertainty inside a task amount, or compare current information with an undocumented old number. Students who can distinguish estimates, baselines, and reserves can read a planning case critically without assuming a framework determines a real organization's approvals or purchases.
learningObjectives: Distinguish a cost estimate, project budget, and cost baseline.
Explain why a time-phased cost baseline can support comparison without predicting the future.
Distinguish contingency reserve from management reserve using PMI's bounded terminology.
Calculate a clearly labeled hypothetical aggregation of estimated work, contingency reserve, and management reserve.
Identify assumptions and scope limits that affect interpretation of a budget model.

collegeVersion.heading: A budget organizes estimates; it is not a forecast guarantee
collegeVersion.body:
A cost estimate is a reasoned approximation based on current information and assumptions. Budgeting organizes such estimates into a plan that can be examined as a whole. GAO's Cost Estimating and Assessment Guide treats purpose, scope, schedule, technical baseline, assumptions, data, methodology, risk and uncertainty, documentation, and updates as connected parts of cost estimating. A total is therefore meaningful only with a stated scope, time basis, and explanation of the estimates being aggregated.

A project budget is often discussed as the total planned amount for a defined project context. A cost baseline is more specific. PMI's lexicon defines it as the approved, time-phased project budget used for comparison with actual results, excluding management reserves. Time-phased means that the plan connects expected amounts to periods or scheduled work rather than leaving every amount in one undated total. The terms approved, baseline, and actual can have organization-specific consequences outside this lesson; the transferable idea is that a reference plan makes comparison possible.

A baseline is neither a guarantee nor a substitute for interpretation. A difference may reflect an inaccurate estimate, changed scope, timing differences, or an assumption that no longer holds. Comparison identifies a question; it does not establish a cause, authorize a change, or direct anyone to spend funds.

collegeVersion.heading: Reserve labels make uncertainty visible rather than invisible
collegeVersion.body:
Project terminology often distinguishes two kinds of planned allowance. In PMI's cost-baseline terminology, contingency reserve is included in the cost baseline for identified risks that have planned responses, while management reserve is excluded from the cost baseline and added to it to form the project budget. This lesson uses that relationship only as a framework-specific conceptual distinction; an organization may use different labels, authority rules, or accounting treatment.

The point is not that every project needs a particular percentage or that a reader should fund anything. An uncertainty allowance should not be silently disguised as an ordinary work estimate. A documented contingency reserve should name the uncertainty or risk context it is intended to address. A management reserve should remain distinct when a framework treats it as outside the baseline. Neither label makes uncertainty disappear, proves that a reserve will be used, or guarantees that it will be sufficient.

An identified risk is a possible future condition, not an existing cost already known to be required. If work is already defined and included in scope, presenting its expected cost as a vague reserve can obscure the model. Decisions about authorization, control, and scope changes require the governing context and responsible people; they are not determined by this general-education lesson.

collegeVersion.heading: A small model shows the relationships, not a real financial decision
collegeVersion.body:
Consider a hypothetical student exhibit. Its planning model contains estimated design work of $900 and estimated display materials of $600. The base estimate is $900 + $600 = $1,500. The model separately records a $150 contingency reserve tied to an identified possibility that an accessible alternate format may need additional materials. Under the PMI relationship used here, the illustrative cost baseline is $1,500 + $150 = $1,650. The case also displays a separately labeled $200 management reserve; adding it produces an illustrative project-budget total of $1,850.

The arithmetic is simple, but the labels do the teaching. The $1,650 baseline is the comparison reference in the example; the $200 management reserve is not inside that baseline. The model assumes the work estimates are complete for this narrow illustration, the contingency concerns a possible rather than already-required addition, and the management reserve is treated separately under PMI terminology. It excludes taxes, vendor terms, funding, approvals, procurement, and actual spending.

No universal reserve percentage can be inferred from this example. Better questions are: What work is estimated? What is included and excluded? What uncertainty is being labeled? What time period does the reference plan cover? What does a change from the reference mean in this context? Those questions improve transparency while leaving real financial and organizational decisions to the appropriate process.

vocabulary.definition: A reasoned approximation of the cost of defined work, based on current information and assumptions.
A stated total plan for project costs in a particular context; its exact composition depends on the framework and organization.
In PMI terminology, the approved time-phased project budget used for comparison with actual results and excluding management reserves.
Connected to planned periods or scheduled work rather than expressed only as one undated total.
In PMI terminology, an allowance within the cost baseline for identified risks with planned contingent or mitigating responses.
In PMI terminology, an allowance outside the cost baseline that is added to it to form the project budget.
A difference between a reference plan and current information; it requires interpretation and does not automatically explain itself.
A condition treated as true in a planning model even though later evidence may change it.

eli10.simplifiedExplanation:
A budget model is like planning supplies for a class art project. First, you list the things you expect to need. Then you put the amounts together so everyone can see the plan. You can also label a small just-in-case-this-known-problem-happens amount instead of hiding it inside paint or paper. A baseline is the saved version of the plan you can look back at later to notice what changed.

The saved plan is not magic money and it cannot tell you what to do if something changes. A separately labeled reserve is not extra permission to buy anything. It is simply a way to show which part of a hypothetical plan is for expected work and which part is connected to uncertainty.
eli10.analogy: A budget model is like a labeled packing list for a camping trip: listed gear represents expected needs, a clearly labeled spare item represents a known concern, and the saved list lets you compare the plan with what changed.
eli10.analogyLimits: Projects may involve time-phased work, estimates, uncertainty, authority, and formal accounting that a camping list does not capture. The analogy cannot decide a real purchase, reserve level, approval, or organizational policy.

workedExample: A student exhibit is a hypothetical planning case. Estimated design work is $900 and estimated display materials are $600, so its base estimate is $1,500. The model adds a separately labeled $150 contingency reserve for the identified possibility that accessible alternate-format materials may require extra supplies. Its illustrative cost baseline is therefore $1,650. It separately shows a $200 management reserve, making the illustrative project-budget total $1,850. The example uses PMI's baseline relationship, does not recommend any reserve amount, and excludes actual purchasing, taxes, vendor terms, funding, approvals, and financial advice.

commonMistakes.mistake: Calling any total a baseline.
commonMistakes.correction: A baseline is a defined reference plan; explain its scope, time basis, and what it excludes.

commonMistakes.mistake: Hiding uncertainty inside an ordinary work estimate.
commonMistakes.correction: Label the assumption or risk context and distinguish it from known, defined work.

commonMistakes.mistake: Treating contingency and management reserve as automatic synonyms.
commonMistakes.correction: State which framework's terminology is being used and whether the amount is inside or outside the baseline.

commonMistakes.mistake: Assuming a variance tells a complete story.
commonMistakes.correction: A difference from a baseline prompts investigation; it does not prove a cause or prescribe a response.

commonMistakes.mistake: Turning a hypothetical model into spending advice.
commonMistakes.correction: Keep examples illustrative and leave real approvals, procurement, funding, and accounting to their governing context.

compareContrast.distinction: An estimate approximates defined work; a cost baseline is a time-phased reference budget assembled for comparison.
In PMI terminology, management reserve is excluded from the cost baseline but added to it to form the project budget.
In PMI terminology, contingency reserve sits within the baseline for identified-risk responses, while management reserve is held outside the baseline.

keyTakeaway: Budgeting makes the relationship among estimates, timing, and stated uncertainty inspectable. A cost baseline gives a reference for comparison, while clearly labeled contingency and management reserves preserve the distinction between defined work and uncertainty. None of these concepts guarantees a result or replaces context-specific financial decisions.

questionBank.prompt: Which statement best describes a cost baseline in the PMI terminology used in this lesson?
options: Any rough total written before project work begins.
A reserve used only for existing, known costs.
An approved, time-phased project budget used for comparison with actual results and excluding management reserves.
A guarantee that actual costs will equal the planned total.
questionBank.explanation: The PMI definition makes the baseline a time-phased reference for comparison and excludes management reserves. It is not a rough total or a guarantee.
questionBank.skill: Recall the bounded PMI definition of a cost baseline.

questionBank.prompt: In the hypothetical exhibit model, what is the cost baseline when base estimates are $1,500 and the separately labeled contingency reserve is $150?
questionBank.explanation: The illustrative baseline is the $1,500 base estimate plus the $150 contingency reserve, or $1,650. The separately displayed $200 management reserve is outside that baseline.
questionBank.skill: Apply the lesson's labeled hypothetical aggregation.

questionBank.prompt: Which label most accurately fits an amount for a defined piece of work already included in the current scope?
options: A cost estimate for that defined work.
Management reserve, solely because the work costs money.
Contingency reserve, even though the work is already known to be required.
A variance, because it appears in a plan.
questionBank.explanation: Defined work belongs in the model's estimate. A reserve is used to label uncertainty under the relevant framework; a variance is a difference from a reference, not a work category.
questionBank.skill: Distinguish defined work from a reserve or a variance.

questionBank.prompt: Why can comparing current information with a cost baseline be useful without deciding what action to take?
options: It makes every underlying cause of a difference obvious.
It makes the original estimate permanent.
It makes financial approval unnecessary.
It makes a difference from the reference plan visible, while the cause and response still require context.
questionBank.explanation: A baseline supports comparison. The reason for a difference and any response depend on evidence, context, authority, and the applicable process.
questionBank.skill: Analyze the limit of a baseline comparison.

questionBank.prompt: Which practice best preserves transparency about uncertainty in a budget model?
options: Include every possible future cost in one unlabeled task estimate.
State the modeled work, assumptions, exclusions, and separately labeled reserve relationship.
Treat a reserve as proof that a risk will occur.
Use one fixed reserve percentage for every project without examining its context.
questionBank.explanation: A transparent model names its scope, assumptions, exclusions, and uncertainty. That information supports interpretation without predicting the future or prescribing a reserve amount.
questionBank.skill: Identify transparent documentation of estimates and uncertainty.

provenance.rightsStatus: original-synthesis
provenance.scopeNote: General education about estimate aggregation, time-phased cost baselines, and reserve terminology. It excludes personal or organizational financial advice, funding, procurement, vendor selection, taxes, accounting treatment, approvals, and actual spending.

title: Resource Planning
in30Seconds: Resource planning identifies the people, equipment, materials, facilities, and other assets a project activity needs, then compares that need with what is actually available at the needed time. It is not simply assigning a name to a task. A useful plan records the required capability, quantity, timing, constraints, and assumptions. Capacity is the usable amount of a resource over a period; availability is the portion that can realistically be used for this work. When demand exceeds either one, the plan exposes a tradeoff to examine rather than pretending the resource is unlimited.
whyItMatters: A schedule can look feasible while silently assuming the same specialist, room, tool, or material is available for several activities at once. Resource planning makes those assumptions visible before work begins or changes. It helps learners distinguish a role from a particular person, a resource’s theoretical capacity from its available time, and a skill requirement from a job title. The point is not to maximize every resource or prescribe staffing decisions. It is to build a reasoned, revisable picture of what work needs, when it needs it, and which constraints may affect the plan.
learningObjectives: Define resource planning and distinguish resource need, capacity, and availability.
Identify people, equipment, materials, facilities, and information as possible project resources.
Describe how task timing, quantity, capability, and constraints shape a resource need.
Compare a role or skill requirement with the assignment of a particular person.
Analyze a simple capacity conflict and name context-dependent tradeoffs without giving staffing advice.

collegeVersion.heading: Resource planning connects work to finite inputs
collegeVersion.body:
Resource planning asks what is needed to perform each part of a project and when it will be needed. OpenStax describes it as determining needed resources and timing while assessing availability and allocation. The resources are not only people. Depending on the work, they may include equipment, materials, facilities, data, software access, or a specialized service. A project renovating a classroom, for example, might need a technician with electrical knowledge, a room available during a limited window, ladders, replacement fixtures, and access to the building plan. Naming the deliverable alone does not reveal those inputs.

A concise resource entry can state the activity, resource type, required capability or specification, quantity, time window, and relevant assumption. “Two design hours” is weak if the work requires a particular accessibility-review skill or if the two hours must occur before a dependent activity. “One projector” is incomplete if the projector must be compatible with a specific room or available on a particular date. Detail should serve an identifiable planning question; a long inventory with no link to work is not automatically useful.

Project work is often decomposed before resource needs are considered. A work breakdown structure or activity list makes it easier to ask what each defined piece needs. This does not mean a resource plan becomes a universal template. Predictive, iterative, and hybrid projects may revisit needs at different intervals. The transferable idea is to connect each current resource assumption to a piece of work and a time period so it can be reviewed when either changes.

collegeVersion.heading: Capacity, availability, and capability are different checks
collegeVersion.body:
Capacity is the amount of a resource that could be used over a stated period under an explicit planning model. For a meeting room, it might be its open time during a week. For a piece of equipment, it might be usable hours after maintenance windows. For people, capacity is not a claim about personal worth or a direction about anyone’s workload; in a classroom model, it is a bounded planning input that must account for known assignments, absences, and other constraints.

Availability is narrower: the amount of that capacity that can actually be used by this project in the relevant window. A video-editing suite may have twenty possible hours in a week but only four available before a project’s review session because other work already occupies it. A person can have relevant knowledge yet not be available during the required period. Conversely, an available resource may lack the needed capability. Resource planning therefore tests three separate questions: Is there enough of the resource? Is it free when the work needs it? Does it meet the needed specification or skill?

For people, plan from work needs and roles rather than assumptions about a named individual. A role describes a kind of contribution, such as a reviewer who can check captions for accessibility. A skill requirement describes the capability needed for that contribution. Assigning a particular person is a context-sensitive organizational decision outside this lesson. The educational point is that a job title by itself may not demonstrate the required skill, and a skilled person’s existence does not demonstrate their availability. This distinction can prevent a schedule from treating “someone will handle it” as evidence.

collegeVersion.heading: Conflicts expose tradeoffs; they do not supply one automatic answer
collegeVersion.body:
Resource demand is the amount of a resource the planned work calls for in a period. A conflict appears when overlapping work asks for more than available capacity, or when the required capability, equipment, material, or facility is unavailable at the needed time. Consider a hypothetical student exhibit. Two teams each need the single photo printer for three hours on Tuesday afternoon, but the printer can only be used by one team at a time. The request is six printer-hours in one three-hour window, so the current plan has a timing conflict. The arithmetic identifies the issue; it does not decide whose work matters more.

Possible planning responses can include moving nondependent work, changing the sequence, reducing or redefining work after appropriate review, finding an equivalent resource, or recognizing that a milestone may need reconsideration. Each carries a tradeoff. Moving work can affect dependencies; substituting equipment can affect quality or compatibility; reducing work can affect scope; changing timing can affect access or other planned activities. A responsible lesson should not tell a real organization which option to choose, hire, purchase, or authorize. Instead, it teaches learners to state the constraint, assumptions, affected work, and consequences that decision-makers would need to examine.

Resource information needs updates when the project’s work, timing, condition, or known availability changes. A plan is useful because it is explicit and revisable, not because it eliminates uncertainty. It should not be read as an employment recommendation, a procurement instruction, a budget, or a guarantee that a project will finish as planned.

vocabulary.definition: Identifying the inputs project work needs, when they are needed, and the constraints affecting their use.
A documented need for a resource type, quantity, capability, specification, or time window connected to project work.
The usable amount of a resource under a stated planning model during a defined period.
The portion of a resource’s capacity that can realistically be used for the relevant work and time window.
A skill, qualification, feature, compatibility condition, or other property required for a resource to perform the work.
A defined kind of contribution to project work, separate from the choice of a particular person.
A mismatch in which planned demand exceeds usable availability or the required capability is missing.

eli10.simplifiedExplanation:
Resource planning is like preparing for a school play. You need actors, costumes, a stage, lights, and time to practice. It is not enough to say, “We need lights.” You also need to know which lights, how many, and whether the stage has them on the rehearsal day. A person who knows how to run lights might already be busy during that time, so having the skill and being free are different things.

Capacity is like the number of seats on the school bus. Availability is how many of those seats are not already taken for this trip. If two groups both need the same costume rack at the same time, the plan has a conflict. The conflict is useful information: the groups may need different times or another way to do the work.
eli10.analogy: Resource planning is like packing supplies for a model-building day. You list the glue, blocks, table space, and helpers each model needs, then check whether they are ready when each group starts.
eli10.analogyLimits: Project resources can involve changing requirements, specialized skills, access rules, and dependencies. A supply list cannot decide real workplace assignments, purchases, or priorities.

workedExample: A campus museum hypothetically plans two digital-display updates. Each update needs a technician who can operate the display software for two hours on Wednesday morning. Only one qualified technician is available in that four-hour window. The total demand is 2 + 2 = 4 technician-hours, which equals the available hours, so the work can fit only if the activities do not overlap and no setup, interruption, or other assignment consumes that window. The resource entry should also note the required software skill and the assumed availability. If the updates must occur simultaneously, the schedule has a capability-and-timing conflict; simply listing “one technician” does not resolve it. The example does not recommend a staffing action or promise that either update will occur.

commonMistakes.mistake: Treating capacity as availability.
commonMistakes.correction: Record the relevant time window and other known uses before assuming a resource can be used.

commonMistakes.mistake: Using a title as proof of a required skill.
commonMistakes.correction: Describe the capability or specification the work needs, then verify it separately from a role label.

commonMistakes.mistake: Listing resources without linking them to work and timing.
commonMistakes.correction: Connect each resource requirement to an activity, quantity, time window, and assumption.

commonMistakes.mistake: Assuming a conflict has one universal fix.
commonMistakes.correction: Make the constraint and affected work visible, then compare context-dependent tradeoffs rather than prescribing a staffing, purchasing, or priority decision.

compareContrast.distinction: Capacity is usable amount in a defined period; availability is the portion actually free for the relevant work and time.
A role names a kind of contribution; capability names the skill, feature, or condition needed to make that contribution.
A requirement states what work needs; an assignment links a specific resource to it in a particular context.

keyTakeaway: Resource planning turns project work into explicit, time-bound needs for finite people, equipment, materials, facilities, and other inputs. By checking capability, capacity, and availability separately, learners can recognize conflicts and describe tradeoffs without treating a preliminary plan as a guarantee or directive.

questionBank.prompt: What is the best description of resource planning?
options: Choosing a project’s final budget without considering work.
Assigning every task to a named employee as early as possible.
Identifying what project work needs and when, then comparing those needs with available resources.
Guaranteeing that every project resource will be used continuously.
questionBank.explanation: Resource planning connects defined work and timing to the needed resources, then considers actual availability and constraints. It does not guarantee continuous use or prescribe named assignments.
questionBank.skill: Recall the definition and purpose of resource planning.

questionBank.prompt: Which statement correctly distinguishes capacity from availability?
options: Capacity applies only to people, while availability applies only to equipment.
Availability is always larger than capacity.
Capacity is a required skill, while availability is a role title.
Capacity is usable amount in a period; availability is the portion free for the relevant work and time.
questionBank.explanation: Capacity is the modeled usable amount during a stated period. Availability is the narrower amount actually free for this project when it needs the resource.
questionBank.skill: Distinguish resource capacity from project-specific availability.

questionBank.prompt: A project needs three identical microphones for a recording session, but only two compatible microphones are available then. What does this show?
options: A resource conflict: the available compatible quantity is below the planned demand.
Proof that the project’s scope is complete.
That the microphones have unlimited capacity if the team waits.
That a named person must be reassigned.
questionBank.explanation: The planned demand is three compatible microphones, while only two are available in the required window. That mismatch is a resource conflict, not a staffing instruction.
questionBank.skill: Identify a quantity-and-timing resource conflict.

questionBank.prompt: Why should a plan state a required capability separately from a role title?
options: A role title automatically guarantees every needed skill.
A title does not by itself show that a resource has the specific skill, feature, or compatibility needed for the work.
Capability is only relevant after a project is finished.
Roles and capabilities always mean exactly the same thing.
questionBank.explanation: A role is a kind of contribution, while capability is the particular skill, feature, or condition the work requires. A title alone does not establish either that capability or timing availability.
questionBank.skill: Analyze why role labels and required capabilities are distinct planning inputs.

questionBank.prompt: Two activities require the same single testing room at the same time. Which response best reflects sound resource-planning reasoning?
options: Assume both can use the room because the room is listed in the plan.
Declare that one activity must be cancelled without examining consequences.
Record the timing conflict, affected activities, and assumptions, then examine alternatives and their tradeoffs.
Treat the room’s physical existence as proof of availability.
questionBank.explanation: A sound plan first makes the finite-room conflict explicit and examines alternatives with their consequences. The example supplies no universal priority, purchase, or staffing decision.
questionBank.skill: Choose an evidence-based response to a shared-resource timing conflict.

provenance.rightsStatus: original-synthesis
provenance.scopeNote: General education about people, equipment, materials, facilities, availability, capacity, capability, and planning tradeoffs. It excludes employment, procurement, budget, stakeholder, legal, financial, or organization-specific advice.

title: Stakeholders
in30Seconds: Stakeholders are people, groups, or institutions that can affect a project, are affected by it, or have a legitimate interest in its result. Identifying them means looking beyond the project team to understand relevant users, operators, sponsors, partners, and others. Interests, influence, and impact help a team ask better questions; they do not rank human worth or give anyone automatic control. Respectful, honest, context-aware communication keeps useful information visible.
whyItMatters: Projects can miss important needs when they focus only on the people funding or building a result. A stakeholder perspective helps learners notice who may use, maintain, depend on, be burdened by, or make decisions about a change. It also discourages a common mistake: treating communication as persuasion. Good engagement is a two-way effort to understand relevant information, explain what is known and unknown, and make room for concerns without promising agreement or a particular outcome.
learningObjectives: Define stakeholder in a project context.
Identify different ways a person or group can be connected to a project.
Distinguish interest, influence, impact, and formal decision authority.
Apply ethical and context-aware communication principles to a hypothetical project.
Explain why stakeholder information should be revisited as evidence changes.

collegeVersion.heading: Stakeholders are connected to a project in more than one way
collegeVersion.body:
A stakeholder is a person, group, or institution that can affect a project, can be affected by it, or has a legitimate interest in its result. The definition is deliberately broader than the project team. A funder, sponsor, staff member, user, neighboring community, partner organization, regulator, maintenance group, or service recipient may each be connected differently. Not every possible connection is equally relevant to every project, and the list should be based on evidence rather than assumptions. The point is to look for material relationships that a narrow team-only view might miss.

Identification is therefore an inquiry, not a ceremony. A project may examine its purpose, intended result, current situation, likely users, operating environment, dependencies, and foreseeable effects. It can ask who provides needed information, who will operate or support the result, who may experience a benefit or burden, and who has formal responsibility for a decision. These questions are useful even when the team does not yet know the answer. An unknown affected group or an unresolved constraint is information to investigate, not an excuse to declare the analysis finished.

Being named as a stakeholder does not mean a person has the same role as a sponsor or a formal decision maker. It also does not mean every preference becomes a requirement. A person who uses a service may have first-hand knowledge of a problem; an operator may know a practical constraint; a decision maker may have authority established elsewhere. These are different kinds of relevance. Keeping them distinct avoids two errors: excluding someone because they lack formal power, and implying that informal influence automatically creates decision authority.

collegeVersion.heading: Interest, influence, and impact are lenses, not labels for controlling people
collegeVersion.body:
Stakeholder analysis often considers interests, influence, and impact. Interest asks what outcome, concern, responsibility, or information need is relevant to a stakeholder. Influence asks how a person or group may affect the project or its environment, for example through knowledge, resources, authority, cooperation, public response, or control of a dependency. Impact asks how the project may change a stakeholder's work, access, safety, time, costs, or experience. None of these is a measure of a person's value, and none alone answers what the project should do.

A simple stakeholder record might name a group, describe its connection to the project, note what is known and uncertain, and identify an appropriate opportunity for information exchange. It is a working model, not a psychological profile. Recording that transit riders may need clear outage information, for example, is different from guessing what they will support. Recording that an operations team will maintain a service is different from deciding that team must accept an untested plan. Evidence, humility, and clear limits matter because a project team can easily turn a descriptive map into an unjustified story about people.

Conflicting interests are normal. A proposed change may make a service easier for one set of users while adding work for operators, or it may give a sponsor a desired result while introducing a concern for a community. Listing those differences does not settle the tradeoff. It makes the tradeoff discussable and clarifies what additional evidence may be needed. This general-education lesson does not tell an organization who has final authority, how to negotiate a dispute, or which concern must prevail. It teaches the prior analytical step: do not hide relevant effects or constraints by acting as if only one viewpoint exists.

collegeVersion.heading: Engagement and communication should be honest, accessible, and adaptable
collegeVersion.body:
Engagement means creating a way to exchange relevant information with stakeholders, not simply sending announcements. The information and method should fit the context. A person who needs to make a decision may need an accurate summary of options, assumptions, and unresolved risks. People who will use a result may be able to describe conditions a design review cannot reveal. People who will operate it may identify training, handoff, or maintenance constraints. Communication may need attention to accessibility, language, timing, privacy, security, and the difference between a proposal and a final decision. These are prompts for context-sensitive judgment, not a universal checklist.

Ethical engagement avoids manipulation. A team should not present uncertain claims as settled, bury a material concern in jargon, collect input it never intends to consider, or describe disagreement as a personal defect. It should distinguish what is known, what is proposed, what is outside the project boundary, and what remains open. Respect does not require promising that every request will be adopted. It does require treating people as sources of relevant experience and information rather than obstacles to overcome. A clear explanation of a boundary or uncertainty can be more honest than false reassurance.

Stakeholder information can change. A new dependency may bring in an operator, testing may reveal an accessibility condition, or a planned result may affect a group in a way no one recognized initially. Revisiting the analysis can make these changes visible. It cannot guarantee consensus, prevent conflict, or ensure project success. Nor does it replace the separate work of requirements, risk management, communication planning, or change control. Its value is narrower and foundational: a project has a better basis for learning when it can state who may be connected to the work, what is known about that connection, and how it will seek relevant information without pretending to control people.

vocabulary.definition: A person, group, or institution that can affect a project, is affected by it, or has a legitimate interest in its result.
The ongoing work of finding and describing materially relevant connections between a project and people, groups, or institutions.
A relevant concern, desired outcome, responsibility, or information need connected to a project.
A way a person or group may affect a project or its environment through authority, knowledge, resources, cooperation, or another connection.
A change a project may cause in a stakeholder’s work, access, experience, responsibilities, or circumstances.
A two-way process for exchanging relevant project information and learning from stakeholder input.
Decision-making power assigned by an organization, rule, agreement, or other governing arrangement.

eli10.simplifiedExplanation:
Imagine a school wants to change how students receive weather closure notices. The project team is not the only group that matters. Students and families need messages they can understand. Teachers may need to know when the message changes a schedule. The technology staff may need to keep the system working. Some people may use screen readers or speak another language at home. All of them can be stakeholders because the project affects them or they can provide information about what will work.

The team should not make a list just to decide who to convince. It should learn what different people need to know, what problems they might experience, and what is still uncertain. A principal may have authority to make a decision, but a student still has valuable knowledge about whether a message is understandable. Listening does not promise that every idea wins. It helps the team make its reasoning more honest.
eli10.analogy: A stakeholder map is like a map of a neighborhood before planning a parade. It shows streets, homes, bus stops, and people who may be affected. The map helps planners ask whom to inform and what routes or access needs to consider; it is not a scorecard for deciding whose voice matters most.
eli10.analogyLimits: People are not streets on a map. Their interests can change, they can disagree, and a diagram cannot reveal everything about their experience. The analogy also does not decide who has legal or organizational authority or how a real dispute should be resolved.

workedExample: A city library hypothetically plans to replace paper-only event notices with a web page and optional text alerts. Initial stakeholder identification includes visitors who use the events, staff who update schedules, people who use assistive technology, volunteers who help at events, and the team that maintains the website. The group records different connections: visitors need timely, understandable information; staff need a workable way to correct an event change; the accessibility reviewer can test whether the page can be used with a keyboard and screen reader; and the website team knows technical constraints. It does not assume that the loudest request is the best solution or that any one group has authority to approve every choice. It communicates that the plan is a proposal, asks for feedback on access needs and update timing, and records unanswered questions for later requirements and testing work.

commonMistakes.mistake: Listing only the sponsor and project team as stakeholders.
commonMistakes.correction: Look for people and groups who use, operate, support, decide about, depend on, or are materially affected by the result.

commonMistakes.mistake: Treating influence as proof that someone’s view is automatically correct.
commonMistakes.correction: Use influence as a reason to understand a connection, then examine evidence, authority, impact, and uncertainty separately.

commonMistakes.mistake: Using engagement to pressure people into agreement.
commonMistakes.correction: Communicate honestly, invite relevant information, and distinguish listening from promising a particular outcome.

commonMistakes.mistake: Treating a stakeholder record as permanent.
commonMistakes.correction: Revisit it when the project, its evidence, or its likely effects change.

compareContrast.distinction: Interest describes a relevant concern or information need; formal authority is assigned power to make or approve a decision.
Influence concerns how a stakeholder may affect the project; impact concerns how the project may affect that stakeholder.
Engagement seeks two-way understanding and exchange of relevant information; persuasion seeks to change another person’s view or action.

keyTakeaway: Stakeholder work begins by identifying material connections between a project and the people or groups around it. Interests, influence, impact, and authority are distinct lenses; ethical engagement uses them to learn and communicate honestly, not to manipulate or guarantee agreement.

questionBank.prompt: Which description best fits a project stakeholder?
options: A person, group, or institution that can affect a project, is affected by it, or has a legitimate interest in its result.
Only a paid member of the project team.
Only the person with final approval authority.
Any person who hears about the project.

options: The museum director can authorize the project.

questionBank.prompt: What is the most ethical purpose of a stakeholder record?

title: Communication Planning
in30Seconds: Communication planning is the deliberate design of how project information will move among the people affected by the work. It connects an audience's information need to a message, channel, timing, owner, and way to ask questions or confirm understanding. A good plan does not mean sending more updates. It makes each communication purposeful, understandable, accessible, and appropriately limited when information is sensitive. It is a living coordination aid, not a guarantee that everyone has read or agreed with a message.
whyItMatters: Projects depend on people making compatible decisions with incomplete and changing information. Without a communication plan, an urgent decision can be buried in a broad update, a remote participant can miss a live discussion, or a stakeholder can receive details they do not need. Planning makes those choices visible enough to examine: who needs what, by when, in what form, and how questions will return. It also treats accessibility and privacy as design constraints rather than afterthoughts. These habits help students analyze project coordination without promising an organization-specific process or outcome.
learningObjectives: Define communication planning as a set of purposeful decisions about project information and its exchange.
Distinguish an audience's information need from a channel, a cadence, and a feedback mechanism.
Explain why synchronous and asynchronous channels create different participation conditions.
Apply a minimal, hypothetical communication design while considering accessibility, privacy, and uncertainty.
Evaluate whether a proposed update is appropriately targeted and usable rather than merely frequent.

collegeVersion.heading: Plan the exchange, not just the announcement
collegeVersion.body:
Communication planning is a way to make information flow intentional. At its simplest, it asks: Who is the audience? What decision, action, awareness, or record does that audience need? What message will meet that need? When must it arrive? Which channel is suitable? Who prepares or sends it? How can recipients ask questions, correct a misunderstanding, or show that a response is needed? The resulting plan may be a short working list or a more formal artifact, but its value comes from connecting those choices. A calendar full of meetings or a shared folder full of files is not, by itself, a communication plan.

Audience is more precise than a generic label such as "stakeholders." Different people can be affected by the same project yet need different information. A contributor may need a clear next handoff and its date; a decision maker may need the decision, options, assumptions, and deadline; someone affected by a change may need a plain-language explanation of what will change and where to seek help. Sending each group the same large update can hide the relevant point. The lesson on Stakeholders addresses how people and groups may be identified and considered. This lesson begins after that analysis: it turns distinct information needs into a deliberate exchange.

A message should match its purpose. A status update can summarize current conditions and unresolved issues. A decision request should state the decision needed, relevant context, available choices where appropriate, and the time by which a reply is useful. A record of a decision should preserve what was decided, by whom, when, and any stated follow-up. These categories can overlap, but naming the purpose helps prevent a common failure: presenting information without making clear whether readers are being asked to act, decide, review, or simply stay informed. Communication planning supports coordination; it cannot prove that a message was understood, that a decision was sound, or that all conflict has disappeared.

The plan should also have a review point. Information needs change when the work, risks, participants, or decision paths change. Revisiting a plan does not require a fixed corporate ritual. It means comparing the intended exchange with what is actually happening: Are questions arriving too late? Is a key decision being repeated because its record is hard to find? Are people receiving updates they cannot use? Those observations can justify a small, documented adjustment.

collegeVersion.heading: Choose channel and cadence for the need and the constraints
collegeVersion.body:
A channel is the route through which a message travels, such as a live meeting, phone or video call, shared document, email, or project workspace. Cadence is the planned timing or recurrence of an exchange, such as before a milestone, after a decision, weekly while a condition remains unresolved, or only when a defined trigger occurs. Neither is automatically good. The useful choice depends on the message's purpose, urgency, complexity, need for discussion, need for a durable record, and the practical access conditions of the audience. A channel choice is therefore a reasoned match, not a technological preference.

The Kirkwood Community College project-management OER distinguishes synchronous communication, in which participants take part at the same time, from asynchronous communication, which does not require simultaneous participation. A live discussion can make rapid clarification possible; it can also exclude or burden people who cannot attend at that time because of time zones, schedules, connectivity, caregiving, disability access needs, or other constraints. An asynchronous written update may give people time to read, reflect, and respond; it may be too slow for a time-sensitive question. Many situations benefit from a combination: discuss a complicated issue live when appropriate, then publish a concise record with the decision, unresolved question, owner, and next checkpoint. The lesson does not prescribe that combination for any real organization.

Cadence should be tied to a reason, not to a habit of broadcasting. A weekly update may be suitable for a rapidly changing hypothetical effort, while a notice tied to a decision or a handoff may be clearer for another. Too little communication can leave people unable to act; too much undifferentiated communication can make an urgent item harder to detect. A plan can state a trigger and response expectation without claiming a universally correct frequency. For example, "send a decision request when an unresolved choice would block the next planned handoff; include a reply-by time" describes a logic for timing. It does not tell any organization how long a reply must take.

Plain language supports channel choice but does not replace it. Digital.gov advises writers to define their audience, organize information, use familiar and direct language, and test whether the intended message is clear. In project communication, this suggests leading with the action or decision, defining necessary technical terms, and separating background from the immediate request. It does not mean removing needed complexity or writing every message at one reading level. The aim is usable understanding for a particular audience.

collegeVersion.heading: Build feedback, accessibility, and responsible information boundaries into the design
collegeVersion.body:
Communication is an exchange, so a plan should include a feedback path. That path may be a designated question channel, a review period, a reply mechanism, a meeting agenda item, or a request for confirmation. The appropriate mechanism depends on the purpose. A message that changes a handoff might need a clear way for the receiving person to flag an obstacle; a broad awareness notice might only need a way to report an error. Feedback is not a vote and confirmation is not proof of agreement. They are ways to surface misunderstandings, missing information, or barriers before they become harder to address.

Accessibility is part of whether information reaches its intended audience. A plan that requires a video update should consider a usable text alternative, captions, or both as relevant to the content and audience. W3C's Web Accessibility Initiative explains that captions provide synchronized text for speech and necessary non-speech audio, and distinguishes same-language captions from translated subtitles. Digital.gov similarly recommends considering target audiences' technical literacy, defining unfamiliar terms, and testing accessibility throughout work rather than at the end. Those sources do not supply a universal checklist for every channel, and this lesson does not offer legal compliance advice. They support the broader planning question: can each intended recipient perceive, understand, and use the material in the chosen format?

Privacy and ethics impose a second boundary: the audience should receive enough information for the stated purpose, but not casually receive sensitive details merely because a channel is convenient. The NIST Privacy Framework describes communication about data-processing purposes, practices, associated privacy risks, and available preferences or requests as part of privacy risk management. For a project lesson, the transferable point is modest: before sharing personal or otherwise sensitive information, identify the purpose, who genuinely needs access, what level of detail is necessary, and the applicable policies or obligations. Do not treat this framework as a legal safe harbor; laws, contracts, professional duties, and organizational policies may require context-specific review.

Consider a hypothetical campus exhibit project. The student design team needs the next handoff date and the current open question; a faculty reviewer needs a short decision request with supporting options; visitors need an accessible notice only after a decision changes public information. The team could plan a shared written decision record after a discussion, a short update before the next handoff, and a place to raise questions. Before attaching a volunteer sign-up sheet to a broad update, it should instead ask whether names and contact details are necessary for that audience. This is an illustration of reasoning, not a template or recommendation for a campus. It shows how audience, need, channel, cadence, feedback, accessibility, and information boundaries fit together.

vocabulary.definition: A documented set of choices about who needs project information, what they need, how it will be exchanged, and how responses are handled.
The specific people or groups a message is intended to reach, considered in relation to their information needs and access conditions.
The particular knowledge, decision context, instruction, or record a person requires to act, decide, review, or stay appropriately informed.
The medium or route used to exchange a message, such as a live meeting, email, shared document, or project workspace.
The planned timing, recurrence, or trigger that determines when a communication is sent, discussed, reviewed, or updated.
An exchange in which participants take part at the same time, such as a live meeting or real-time call.
An exchange that participants can send, read, or respond to at different times, such as a written update or shared record.
A defined way for recipients to ask questions, report an error, raise a concern, or indicate that a response is needed.

eli10.simplifiedExplanation:
Imagine a group building a school garden. People do not all need the same news. Someone ordering seeds needs the final plant list. A teacher approving the garden space needs the question that requires a decision. Families may only need to know when the garden will open. A communication plan writes down those differences before messages start flying around.

It also chooses how and when to share information. A quick live conversation can help with a confusing question. A written note can help people who were absent or need time to read. The plan includes a way to ask questions and checks whether people can actually use the message. If a video contains important instructions, words on the screen or a text version may be needed too.

The plan is not magic. Sending a message does not prove everyone understood it. It gives the group a clearer way to notice confusion, fix errors, and avoid sharing private details with people who do not need them.
eli10.analogy: A communication plan is like labeling and routing packages for a school play. Props go to the stage crew, costume instructions go to performers, and audience directions go to visitors. Each package needs the right destination, timing, and a way to report that it did not arrive or was unclear.
eli10.analogyLimits: Project information is not a physical package. People may interpret the same message differently, need a conversation rather than delivery, or have access needs that change the suitable format. Routing also does not decide whether information should be shared in the first place; privacy and ethical obligations still matter.

workedExample: In a hypothetical student-exhibit project, a proposed display location has an unresolved accessibility question. The student team needs the question, the next handoff date, and a place to add evidence. The faculty reviewer needs a short decision request that states the two location options, the accessibility concern, and when a response would keep the next handoff from being blocked. Visitors do not need that internal debate; if the location changes, they need an accessible public notice. The team schedules a live discussion only for people who must clarify the options, then posts a plain-language decision record in a shared space for others to read later and question. It avoids attaching a volunteer contact list to the broad notice because that information is not needed by visitors. The example is a communication design, not advice for any institution.

commonMistakes.mistake: Calling a list of meeting dates a communication plan.
commonMistakes.correction: Connect each exchange to an audience, information need, purpose, channel, timing, owner, and feedback path.

commonMistakes.mistake: Sending every stakeholder the same detailed update.
commonMistakes.correction: Tailor information to the recipient's legitimate need while preserving an appropriate record for others.

commonMistakes.mistake: Treating a live meeting as automatically inclusive or sufficient.
commonMistakes.correction: Consider access conditions and whether a usable asynchronous record or alternative format is needed.

commonMistakes.mistake: Assuming an email or posted file proves understanding.
commonMistakes.correction: Provide an appropriate mechanism for questions, corrections, or confirmation and review whether the exchange is working.

commonMistakes.mistake: Using convenience as a reason to share sensitive details broadly.
commonMistakes.correction: Identify the purpose, necessary audience, necessary detail, and applicable privacy or ethical constraints before sharing.

compareContrast.distinction: A channel is the route or medium for a message; cadence is the planned timing, recurrence, or trigger for that exchange.
Synchronous exchange requires participants at the same time; asynchronous exchange allows participation at different times.
Delivery shows that a message was sent or made available; understanding requires an audience to be able to perceive, interpret, and use it.

keyTakeaway: Communication planning makes the purpose, audience, channel, timing, feedback path, accessibility needs, and information boundaries of project exchanges explicit. It improves coordination by making those choices reviewable, not by guaranteeing attention, agreement, or a particular project result.

options: A set of deliberate choices about audiences, information needs, messages, channels, timing, and responses.
A list of every software tool used by a team.
A promise that all stakeholders will agree with decisions.
A record containing only the dates of meetings.
questionBank.explanation: A communication plan links a purposeful exchange to audience, information need, channel, timing, and feedback. Tools and meeting dates may appear in a plan, but neither alone defines it, and planning cannot guarantee agreement.

questionBank.prompt: Which choice is an example of cadence rather than a channel?
options: A shared project workspace.
Send a decision request when an unresolved choice would block the next handoff.
A video meeting with live captions.
A written record of decisions.
questionBank.explanation: Cadence concerns when an exchange happens or what triggers it. A workspace, meeting, and written record are channels or formats through which a message can travel.
questionBank.skill: Distinguish communication timing from communication medium.

questionBank.prompt: A remote contributor cannot attend a live discussion about an approved change. Which follow-up best supports a communication plan?
options: Assume the contributor can infer the outcome from later work.
Repeat the entire meeting until every participant attends at once.
Post a concise, accessible decision record with the change, rationale, next action, and a way to ask questions.
Send the contributor every internal file associated with the project.
questionBank.explanation: An accessible asynchronous record can support people who could not attend live, while a question path helps surface misunderstandings. It is more targeted than sending all files and does not assume attendance or inference proves understanding.
questionBank.skill: Apply synchronous and asynchronous communication choices to an access constraint.

questionBank.prompt: Before sharing a project update that includes names and contact details, which question is most responsible?
options: Which channel will make the update spread most widely?
Which color scheme will make the update look most urgent?
Can every recipient be required to reply immediately?

questionBank.explanation: Responsible communication considers purpose, necessary audience, and necessary detail before sharing sensitive information. Wider distribution, urgency styling, or mandatory replies do not establish that disclosure is appropriate.
questionBank.skill: Evaluate a communication choice using privacy and ethical information boundaries.

questionBank.prompt: What is the strongest reason to include a feedback mechanism in a communication plan?
options: It ensures that every recipient approves the message.
It gives recipients a defined way to ask questions, report errors, or flag missing information.
It eliminates the need to make the original message clear.
It replaces the need to decide who needs the information.
questionBank.explanation: Feedback mechanisms help reveal misunderstanding, errors, and unmet information needs. They do not guarantee approval, excuse unclear writing, or substitute for identifying the proper audience.
